title: The Duel Between Elephant and Sparrow
summary: In the fragrant branches of an ancient tamala tree in the Dandaka forest, a devoted pair of tiny sparrows had built their woven nest of g...
keywords: the duel between elephant and sparrow
full_text:
In the fragrant branches of an ancient tamala tree in the Dandaka forest, a devoted pair of tiny sparrows had built their woven nest of grass and feathers. For several seasons they lived in peace, and in the springtime, the hen-sparrow laid a clutch of delicate, speckled eggs, brooding over them with maternal affection while her mate brought sweet seeds and berry juice.

One sweltering noon, a colossal rogue wild elephant named Dantamalla, maddened by the flow of rutting temporal fluids and intoxicated with arrogance, came crashing through the forest, ripping up bamboo thickets and smashing saplings in mindless fury. Seeking shade from the scorching sun, the colossus strode beneath the tamala tree. Seizing the heavy branch containing the sparrow's nest in his massive trunk, he wrenched it from the trunk with a deafening crack and hurled it to the earth.

The branch shattered; the sparrow's fragile nest was crushed, and all the precious eggs were smashed upon the rocks, their golden yolks spilling into the dust.

The hen-sparrow shrieked in unbearable grief, fluttering her wings over the broken shells, while the arrogant elephant trampled past with a contemptuous trumpet, caring nothing for the destruction he had wrought.

Hearing his mate's agonizing laments, the cock-sparrow comforted her: 'Weep not, beloved. Crying over spilled eggs will not restore our children, but retribution will avenge their murder. The tyrant believes he is invincible because of his colossal bulk, but he shall learn that intelligence allied with faithful friends is mightier than a thousand tusks.'

The sparrows flew to their loyal companion, a clever woodpecker named Kashthakuta, and recounted their sorrow. The woodpecker shed tears of sympathy and said: 'Grieve no more, friends. I have two powerful allies in this forest: a buzzing fly named Veenarava and a wise green frog named Meghanada. Let us unite our strengths; four small creatures working in harmony can accomplish what an army cannot.'

The four companions gathered by the lily pond and devised a flawless strategic trap.

First, the fly Veenarava buzzed into the clearing where the rogue elephant stood drowsing in the heat. Settling near the beast's ears, the fly began to hum a sweet, enchanting, melodious drone like the strumming of a celestial veena. Charmed by the soothing lullaby, the elephant closed his heavy eyelids in blissful relaxation.

The instant the tyrant's eyes were closed tight, the woodpecker Kashthakuta swooped down from the branches. With his razor-sharp, iron-hard beak, he struck with blinding speed—peck, peck!—piercing both the elephant's eyeballs, blinding him completely!

Roaring in excruciating agony, the blind colossus stumbled through the forest, unable to see trees, rocks, or ravines. For hours he raged, until burning thirst consumed his parched throat. He bellowed for water, but had no idea which way the river lay.

At that moment, the green frog Meghanada hopped to the edge of a deep, yawning, vertical chasm whose rocky walls dropped hundreds of cubits into a bottomless abyss. Standing on the precipice, Meghanada and his marsh companions began croaking loudly in chorus: 'CROAK! CROAK! CROAK!'

Hearing the loud croaking of frogs, the blind elephant deduced: 'Where frogs croak in chorus, there must be a deep, cool, lotus-filled lake!'

Following the sound of the croaking with eager strides, the blinded beast rushed forward, stepped over the edge of the cliff, and tumbled into the bottomless chasm! He crashed upon the jagged boulders below with bone-shattering force, ending his reign of terror forever.

Perched upon the cliff above, the tiny sparrows, the woodpecker, the fly, and the frog looked down upon their fallen oppressor, singing in victory.

Thus Vishnu Sharma taught:
"Let no colossus boast his strength, his bulk of bone and hide,
Nor trample down the humble nests in arrogance and pride;
For tiny sparrows, frogs, and flies, when bound in purpose true,
Can bring the mountain-crushing beast to ruin through and through."
moral: A coalition of tiny, weak creatures united by justice and intelligence can easily bring down the mightiest colossus.

title: The Shrewd Old Gander
summary: In the spreading crown of a colossal, ancient banyan tree that stood in the middle of a fertile forest dwelt a large flock of wild geese,...
full_text:
In the spreading crown of a colossal, ancient banyan tree that stood in the middle of a fertile forest dwelt a large flock of wild geese, governed by their patriarch, a shrewd and experienced old gander named Sarvajna.

One morning, while preening his silver feathers, the old gander noticed a tiny, tender green tendril of an aerial creeper sprouting from the soil at the very base of the banyan's trunk.

Assembling the flock, Sarvajna pointed down to the seedling and warned: 'Brothers, look at that tiny creeper growing at the foot of our ancestral tree. While it is tender and small, fly down and tear it out by the roots!'

The young geese fluttered their wings and laughed: 'What harm can a tiny, fragile green thread do to our colossal banyan? It is smaller than a blade of grass!'

Sarvajna replied with grave urgency: 'Today it is a fragile thread, but as it drinks the monsoon rains, it will climb the trunk, growing as thick and rough as a knotted hempen rope. Soon, any hunter, fowler, or bandit can use this creeper as a natural ladder to climb into our branches by night and snare us all in our sleep. Destroy it before it acquires strength!'

The young, lazy geese ignored his warning, scoffing at the old gander's anxieties.

Years passed, and Sarvajna's prophecy was fulfilled. Fed by the seasonal rains, the creeper grew into an enormous, woody vine that wrapped around the banyan like a coiled python, its thick loops forming a sturdy stairway leading directly into the highest branches.

One evening, while the geese were away foraging for grain in distant harvest fields, a professional fowler passed the tree. Seeing the thick creeper, the hunter climbed with ease into the upper canopy, spread a massive, fine-meshed hemp net across the roosting boughs, weighted the corners with lead pellets, and climbed down, departing for his hut.

At dusk, the flock of geese returned, tired from their long flight. Alighting upon their customary branches in the gathering dark, every single bird was instantly entangled in the hunter's treacherous cords! The more they flapped their wings and struggled, the tighter the knots bound their necks and pinions.

The young geese wept aloud in terror: 'Alas! We are trapped! Tomorrow morning the fowler will come and slaughter us all! How foolish we were to mock the wisdom of our elder!'

The old gander did not waste time in scolding. 'Grief will not untie these cords,' said Sarvajna. 'If you will obey my instructions without hesitation, we may yet preserve our lives. Tomorrow morning, when the fowler climbs the tree, you must all play dead. Stiffen your legs, close your eyes, droop your necks, and do not twitch a single feather. The fowler will think we died of cold and fright. Because dead birds are worthless for the royal aviary and can be sold only for a copper, he will untie us and toss us to the ground one by one to lighten his load. Remain motionless upon the grass until the very last bird has been thrown down. The instant I whistle a sharp note, let every goose spring into the air and fly with all his might!'

At dawn, the fowler climbed the creeper, his heart singing with anticipation. Finding the entire flock stiff and motionless, he muttered in disgust: 'A plague upon this night! They have all perished of the frost!'

Untying the birds from the mesh, he tossed them down to the grassy earth one by one. True to the gander's orders, every bird lay limp upon the turf, feigning death without moving a quill.

When the fowler untied Sarvajna, the eighty-seventh bird, and tossed him down, the old gander whistled a piercing, clarion signal: 'TWEEET!'

In that single instant, eighty-seven geese sprang to life, beat their powerful wings together with a roar like thunder, and soared into the morning sky in a glorious V-formation, leaving the bewildered fowler staring with an open mouth at his empty tree!

Thus Vishnu Sharma taught:
"The creeping vine of danger grows unheeded at your feet;
He who destroys the emerging snare finds future safety sweet;
Yet if by folly you are trapped within the fowler's mesh,
Swift discipline and presence of mind will win your freedom fresh."
moral: Nip emerging danger in the bud; the tiny seed of peril that is ignored today becomes the fatal snare of tomorrow.

title: The Lion and the Ram
summary: In a rugged mountain valley, a ferocious young lion named Chanda reigned supreme over the forest. Having never wandered beyond his native...
full_text:
In a rugged mountain valley, a ferocious young lion named Chanda reigned supreme over the forest. Having never wandered beyond his native ridges, he was acquainted only with deer, boars, and jackals.

One spring morning, a large, thickset domestic ram, carrying an enormous pair of curled, corrugated horns upon his head, strayed from a nomadic shepherd's flock and wandered into the forest. Finding succulent mountain clover growing in a clearing, the ram began to graze peacefully, snorting loudly through his nostrils and shaking his horned head.

Peering through the bushes, the young lion beheld this extraordinary apparition. Seeing the beast's thick wool, broad forehead, and monstrous curved horns, Chanda backed away in terror, whispering to his companion jackal: 'Look at that terrifying warrior! What formidable beast is this? His skull is armed with two colossal curved battle-axes! Surely he is a predator sent from the netherworld to conquer my kingdom!'

The jackal chuckled softly: 'Sire, do not let appearance deceive you. That creature is nothing more than a sheep—a harmless herbivore who feeds upon grass. His horns are for butting his brothers, not for tearing flesh. Observe his actions before you tremble.'

Concealing himself behind a flowering dhak bush, the lion watched with bated breath.

Presently, the ram lowered his formidable head, extended his soft lips, and began nibbling the tender green shoots of grass with delicate, rhythmic chewing, bleating gently: 'Baaa, baaa.'

Seeing the ferocious 'demon' peacefully munching clover like a common doe, the lion felt his terror turn to righteous scorn. 'A beast that feeds upon grass has no warrior heart!' roared Chanda.

Springing from the thicket with flashing claws, the lion brought down the ram with a single blow, feasting upon the meat and learning that formidable horns cannot compensate for a timid herbivore nature.

Thus Vishnu Sharma taught:
"Judge not the stranger by his crest, his horns, or fierce attire;
For many an armored warrior lacks the true heroic fire;
Examine what his nature eats, and how his spirit feeds,
For true nobility is proven only by his deeds."
moral: Do not judge a creature by its formidable appearance; investigate its habits before you fear its power.

title: Smart the Jackal
summary: In a vast jungle, an exceptionally shrewd jackal named Mahachatura, or Smart, roamed the thickets when he came upon the carcass of a mass...
full_text:
In a vast jungle, an exceptionally shrewd jackal named Mahachatura, or Smart, roamed the thickets when he came upon the carcass of a massive, fat wild buffalo that had died of old age in a sandy clearing. The jackal's belly was hollow, but the buffalo's hide was as tough as seasoned ox-leather, and his weak teeth could not pierce the thick skin.

Sitting by the carcass, Smart pondered how to breach the meat.

Presently, the great lion Pingalaka strode into the clearing, licking his chops. Smart prostrated himself to the earth, folded his paws, and said with exaggerated humility: 'O supreme Monarch of the Forest! I have slain this colossal buffalo with great toil expressly for your royal banquet! Deign to accept this humble offering from your devoted servant!'

The noble lion turned his head with aristocratic pride: 'I am the King of Beasts! I never eat prey slain by another creature. I bestow the entire carcass upon you, honest jackal!' With that, the lion walked away into the forest.

Next, a greedy, treacherous tiger padded into the clearing, sniffing the meat. Smart knew the tiger possessed no noble scruples, so he adopted a different strategy. He greeted the tiger with feigned alarm: 'Uncle, run for your life! The great King of Beasts slew this buffalo and went to the river to drink. Before he departed, he commanded me: "Guard this meat! If any tiger dares to touch a mouthful, tell me, and I will tear his stripes from his flesh!"'

Terrified of the lion's wrath, the cowardly tiger leaped into the bushes and vanished like the wind.

Next, a powerful leopard with razor-sharp claws entered the clearing. Smart thought: 'This beast has sharp teeth that can pierce the tough hide, but he is easily frightened.'

Smart bowed to the leopard: 'Welcome, nephew! You appear exhausted by hunger. This buffalo was slain by the King of Beasts, who has gone to bathe. While he is absent, you may quickly tear open the hide and feast! The instant I see the lion returning through the trees, I will give a sharp bark, and you can escape into the canopy.'

Delighted, the hungry leopard sprang upon the buffalo, sank his sharp fangs into the belly, and ripped the tough hide wide open.

Just as the tender meat was exposed, Smart shrieked at the top of his voice: 'Run, nephew, run! The King of Beasts is coming with his army!'

Panicked, the leopard scrambled up a tall tree and fled along the high branches, leaving the opened carcass completely behind.

Finally, another jackal arrived, hoping to share the spoils. Smart said to himself: 'Toward the lion, I used flattery; toward the tiger, fear; toward the leopard, deceit; but toward an equal, one must use force!'

Smart bristled his fur, bared his sharp fangs, growled fiercely, and attacked the rival jackal with such savage fury that the intruder fled howling into the ravine.

Alone in the clearing, the clever jackal feasted upon the delicious, tender meat for an entire week in luxury and peace.

Thus Vishnu Sharma taught:
"Win over the noble with humble speech and courtly grace;
Defeat the cruel coward by the fear of higher place;
Beguile the foolish glutton with a cunning, poisoned bait;
And crush an equal adversary with decisive weight."
moral: He who understands the psychology of different adversaries can defeat them one by one without striking a blow.

title: The Monk Who Left His Body Behind
summary: In a secluded Himalayan cave dwelt a master yogi who had attained the extraordinary Siddhi of Parakaya Pravesha—the mystical power to det...
keywords: the monk who left his body behind
full_text:
In a secluded Himalayan cave dwelt a master yogi who had attained the extraordinary Siddhi of Parakaya Pravesha—the mystical power to detach his living soul from his physical frame and project it into the body of another creature, while his own body lay dormant like a corpse.

He had a solitary disciple who served him for years with devotion, begging daily to be initiated into the secret mantra of soul-transference. Moved by his disciple's persistent prayers, the guru at last taught him the sacred syllables, but laid upon him this solemn commandment: 'Use this supernatural power only to alleviate the suffering of living beings, and never for personal vanity, greed, or the usurpation of another's form.'

One day, while walking along a mountain trail, they came upon the carcass of a magnificent, royal tusker elephant that had slipped from a cliff. The master, desiring to demonstrate the power of the mantra, said to the disciple: 'Sit beside my dormant body, guard it faithfully from vultures and wild beasts, and do not let a fly touch my limbs. I shall animate this noble elephant for one hour to experience its strength.'

Chanting the secret syllables, the master projected his soul into the great elephant. The colossal beast stirred, opened its amber eyes, trumpeted with joy, and ambled gracefully through the forest.

The disciple, sitting beside his master's motionless body, was seized by dark, venomous ambition: 'Why should I spend my youth as a humble disciple in rags? My master's body is youthful, radiant with yogic splendor, and revered by kings and pilgrims! If I burn my own ugly, weak body and enter my master's frame, I will inherit his fame, his hermitage, and his disciples!'

Chanting the mantra, the treacherous disciple left his own body and entered the master's radiant frame. He immediately cast his old, discarded corpse into a blazing funeral pyre, laughing at his cunning.

Presently, the master's soul returned in the elephant. Finding his human body possessed by the treacherous disciple, who mocked him from the hermitage veranda, the master realized that his own form was lost to him forever.

Yet the master's yogic wisdom did not abandon him. Embracing his colossal elephant form, he reflected: 'The physical body is but a garment of clay, shed like an old cloak. The true spirit remains pure.' Using his mighty elephant strength, the master cleared forests, built mountain bridges for pilgrims, and lived revered by the forest creatures as a saint of the woods, while the treacherous disciple, burdened by unearned spiritual power, soon fell into sensual corruption and perished in disgrace.

Thus Vishnu Sharma taught:
"He who usurps another's frame to seize an unearned name,
Shall find the borrowed splendor turn to misery and shame;
For virtue resides within the soul, and not the shell of clay,
Which time and destiny will strip when falsehood fades away."
moral: He who abandons his secure position to possess another's splendor risks losing both forever.

title: The Girl Who Married a Snake
summary: In the city of Mahilaropya lived an elderly Brahmin couple who had prayed for decades to be blessed with an heir. When at last the wife c...
keywords: the girl who married a snake
full_text:
In the city of Mahilaropya lived an elderly Brahmin couple who had prayed for decades to be blessed with an heir. When at last the wife conceived and gave birth, the child brought forth was not a human babe, but a venomous black serpent!

The horrified neighbors urged the father to destroy the monster immediately, but the maternal heart of the mother cried out: 'He was born of my womb, and I will nourish him as my own son!' She placed the serpent in a cushioned willow basket, fed him bowls of sweetened milk, almonds, and honey, and watched him grow into a massive, glistening cobra.

When the serpent reached adulthood, his mother wept: 'My son is of age; who will find a bride for him?'

The father traveled to a distant city and approached an impoverished, noble Brahmin whose daughter was celebrated for her beauty and filial piety. Without revealing that the groom was a serpent, the father negotiated the marriage and paid a lavish dowry.

When the bridal party arrived and the truth was revealed, the bride's companions cried out in horror, urging the maiden to flee: 'Do not wed this cold-blooded reptile! He will strike you with his venom on your wedding night!'

The virtuous maiden replied with serene dignity: 'My father gave his solemn word of honor, and I will not break his pledge. Whether destiny gives me a prince or a serpent, a dutiful wife accepts her appointed fate with a faithful heart.'

The wedding rituals were performed, and the maiden took up her residence in the bridal chamber, caring for the great cobra with tenderest devotion, feeding him bowls of warm milk and cleaning his wicker basket.

One night, the maiden awoke to the sound of soft footsteps. Looking toward the hearth, she gasped: the shed serpent skin lay discarded upon the floor, and standing before her was a youth of heavenly beauty, crowned with jewels and radiant as the god of love!

The youth smiled gently: 'Beloved wife, your unyielding fidelity has broken the ancient celestial curse that bound me in reptilian form!'

While the prince slept, the maiden carried the empty serpent skin to the brazier and burned it to ashes. Released forever from his scaly prison, the prince revealed his royal lineage to his astonished parents, filling their home with wealth, joy, and eternal honor.

Thus Vishnu Sharma taught:
"The maiden who with steadfast faith accepts her sorrow's share,
And honors vows of duty with a pure and patient prayer,
Transforms the venom of the snake to nectar sweet and bright,
And wakes to find her darkness crowned with everlasting light."
moral: Steadfast devotion and filial duty turn apparent adversity into golden blessing.

title: Poor Blossom
summary: In a quiet glade on the slopes of the Malaya mountains grew a magnificent, ancient flowering champaka tree known to the forest dwellers a...
full_text:
In a quiet glade on the slopes of the Malaya mountains grew a magnificent, ancient flowering champaka tree known to the forest dwellers as Poor Blossom. Every spring, its boughs were covered with thousands of golden, star-shaped blossoms that filled the mountain breezes with an intoxicating, celestial fragrance, attracting swarms of humming bees and singing songbirds.

Weary pilgrims, forest ascetics, and wandering merchants rested beneath its leafy umbrella, finding cool relief from the blazing noon sun.

One scorching afternoon, a crude and greedy woodcutter named Bhima arrived in the glade, panting with exhaustion. He threw down his heavy iron axe, leaned against the scented trunk of Poor Blossom, and drank cool water from a nearby spring. Resting in the fragrant shade, he looked up into the leafy boughs, admiring the golden flowers.

'What a magnificent tree!' thought the woodcutter. 'Its wood must be seasoned, heavy, and fragrant. If I chop down this tree, its timber will yield fine planks for temple chests, and its branches will supply me with firewood for an entire winter!'

Unsheathing his sharp iron axe, the ungrateful man began hacking into the trunk that had just sheltered him from the burning sun. Blow after blow bit into the living wood, spraying sweet-smelling sap upon the grass.

Perched in the upper branches, a golden oriole cried out in horror: 'Madman! What are you doing? This tree gave you cool shade, sweet scent, and sheltered your weary head! Why do you destroy the living sanctuary that comforted you?'

The woodcutter sneered: 'Sentimentality is for birds! Timber is for profit!'

He swung his axe with double fury. As the deep notch cleaved through the heartwood, the ancient tree groaned, trembled, and collapsed with a thunderous roar.

Yet in its fall, the massive, heavy crown of Poor Blossom twisted sideways. A giant bough struck the woodcutter squarely across his spine, crushing his legs and pinning him beneath the splintered trunk. Paralyzed and bleeding in the wilderness, the ungrateful man perished beside the fallen blossoms he had destroyed.

Thus Vishnu Sharma taught:
"He who strikes down the friendly bough that shielded him from heat,
And crushes out the fragrant life that made his resting sweet,
Shall find the falling timber strike his own ungrateful head,
And lie beneath the ruined branch among the withered dead."
moral: He who destroys the very tree that gave him shade and fragrant blossoms acts as his own worst enemy.

title: The Unteachable Monkey
summary: In the high branches of an expansive shami tree on the riverbank lived a flock of industrious, clever weaver-birds. Before the onset of t...
full_text:
In the high branches of an expansive shami tree on the riverbank lived a flock of industrious, clever weaver-birds. Before the onset of the stormy season, each bird had diligently gathered strong fibers of grass, weaving tight, comfortable, flask-shaped nests that hung securely from the twigs, keeping their fledglings warm and dry even during the heaviest downpours.

When the great monsoon clouds gathered, a violent tempest broke over the forest. Thunder shook the hills; sheets of icy rain lashed through the canopy, and freezing winds stripped the leaves from the boughs.

Safe inside their snug, hanging nests, the weaver-birds rested in comfort.

Beneath the shami tree sat a troop of wild monkeys, drenched to the skin, shivering uncontrollably, with their teeth chattering like castanets. Among them was an old monkey who huddled upon a wet bough, whimpering in misery as the icy water soaked into his fur.

Looking out from the dry threshold of her woven nest, a gentle weaver-bird felt compassion for the suffering creature. Calling down politely, she chirped: 'Brother monkey! You possess hands and feet precisely like human beings; you are agile, strong, and capable of climbing any tree. Why did you spend the warm summer days leaping idly from bough to bough, instead of gathering grass and building a sturdy shelter against the storm? Had you built a home, you would not be shivering in this misery!'

Hearing the tiny bird offer him advice, the arrogant monkey took fire with insulted vanity. 'What!' snarled the beast. 'Does this miserable feathered mite, who could fit inside my palm, dare to instruct a lord of the forest on how to live?'

Concealing his fury until the rain slackened, the vicious monkey climbed into the upper branches. He seized the weaver-bird's exquisite nest, tore it to shreds with his claws, crushed the speckled eggs within, and threw the ruined fibers into the muddy stream!

The weeping bird fled to another tree, learning the bitter cost of offering unrequested counsel to a fool.

Thus Vishnu Sharma taught:
"Bestow your counsel on the wise who prize the teacher's word;
Waste not the gems of intellect where folly is preferred;
For he who lectures to a fool who lacks the wit to learn
Shall see his kindness met with wrath and all his shelter torn."
moral: Never offer good advice to an arrogant fool who lacks the wisdom to receive it.

title: Right-Mind and Wrong-Mind
summary: In a prosperous city lived two companions named Dharmabuddhi, or Right-Mind, and Dushtabuddhi, or Wrong-Mind. Right-Mind was honest, virt...
full_text:
In a prosperous city lived two companions named Dharmabuddhi, or Right-Mind, and Dushtabuddhi, or Wrong-Mind. Right-Mind was honest, virtuous, and hardworking, while Wrong-Mind was lazy, envious, and perpetually scheming to live upon the toil of others.

One day, Wrong-Mind proposed: 'Friend, why waste our youth in this city? Let us travel to distant foreign lands, trade with courage, and acquire vast riches so that we may live in comfort in our old age.'

Agreeing to the proposal, Right-Mind set out with him. Through honest enterprise, keen commercial foresight, and diligence, they amassed a fortune of one thousand pure gold dinars and returned toward their native city.

As they reached the forest outskirts, Right-Mind proposed: 'Let us divide our gold equally, five hundred dinars to each, and enter the city rejoicing.'

Wrong-Mind, plotting to steal the whole treasure, said: 'Friend, it is dangerous to carry so much gold into the town; thieves, relatives, and tax collectors will torment us. Let us take one hundred dinars each for immediate expenses, and bury the remaining eight hundred dinars beneath the roots of this ancient, hollow banyan tree. Whenever we need more gold, we will return together and unearth it.'

Trusting his friend, Right-Mind agreed. They buried the eight hundred gold coins in a deep pit beneath the banyan and entered the city.

A few nights later, Wrong-Mind stole into the forest under the cover of darkness, dug up the treasure, pocketed all eight hundred dinars, refilled the pit with earth, and returned home.

A month later, Wrong-Mind approached Right-Mind, saying: 'Brother, my funds are exhausted; let us go to the banyan and divide the remaining gold.'

They dug beneath the roots, but found only an empty pit!

In an instant, Wrong-Mind tore his hair, beat his chest, and screamed: 'Thief! Traitor! You came by night and stole our eight hundred dinars! Divide the gold with me, or I will drag you before the King's magistrates!'

Right-Mind was stunned: 'I have never touched the gold! My name is Right-Mind, and I would rather die than commit a theft!'

They dragged the dispute before the city court. When the judges, unable to decide between their conflicting oaths, ordered the trial by ordeal of fire, Wrong-Mind said: 'Why resort to divine ordeals when a living witness is at hand? The sacred spirit of the banyan tree witnessed our burial of the gold! Let the judges come to the tree tomorrow at dawn and hear the witness of the tree!'

That night, Wrong-Mind concealed his aged father inside the hollow trunk of the banyan tree, instructing him: 'When the judges ask who stole the gold, cry out with a loud voice: "Right-Mind is the thief!"'

At dawn, the magistrates assembled around the banyan. The chief judge called out: 'O sacred Tree Spirit! Reveal the truth: who took the eight hundred gold dinars?'

From the hollow trunk, a trembling voice boomed: 'Hearken, O judges! Right-Mind is the thief who dug up the gold!'

The judges were astounded and prepared to condemn Right-Mind to the gallows.

Right-Mind, however, suspected foul play. Pondering the hollow trunk, he said calmly: 'Before sentence is passed, allow me to perform a sacred purification ritual to honor this miraculous tree spirit.'

Gathering dry thorns, brushwood, and heaps of dry leaves, Right-Mind piled them around the entrance of the hollow trunk and set the brush on fire, fanning the dense, acrid smoke into the cavity.

Within moments, agonizing shrieks echoed from within the trunk. Out tumbled Wrong-Mind's aged father, his clothes on fire, his skin blistered, coughing up blood and soot. Falling before the judges, the dying man confessed the entire criminal conspiracy orchestrated by his wicked son.

The judges condemned Wrong-Mind to be hanged upon the nearest tree, while Right-Mind was awarded the recovered gold and the praise of the entire kingdom.

Thus Vishnu Sharma taught:
"The knave who weaves an evil plot and uses sacred names,
And hides his fraud behind a tree, shall perish in the flames;
For truth unmasks the deepest plot that wicked minds devise,
And justice turns the scheming trap against the lord of lies."
moral: Truth and righteousness triumph over deceit; he who uses his own father in fraud brings ruin upon his house.

title: A Remedy Worse than the Disease
summary: In the high branches of an expansive banyan tree on the shores of a mountain lake dwelt a flock of herons, who raised their broods in pea...
keywords: a remedy worse than the disease
full_text:
In the high branches of an expansive banyan tree on the shores of a mountain lake dwelt a flock of herons, who raised their broods in peace. But in a hollow burrow at the base of the trunk lived a venomous black cobra, who crawled up the bark every season and devoured the newly hatched heron fledglings, leaving the parent birds in despair.

One morning, an old heron sat weeping by the water's edge. A crab crawled out from beneath a stone and inquired: 'Uncle, why do you weep so bitterly?'

The heron recounted how the black snake destroyed their young every year. The crab, who secretly despised the herons because they preyed on his kinsmen, thought: 'Here is an opportunity to destroy both my enemies with a single stroke!'

The crab smiled shrewdly: 'Uncle, I know a sovereign remedy. A family of hungry mongooses dwells in the rocky ridge half a mile away. Mongooses are the natural mortal enemies of cobras. Go to the fish market, purchase fresh fish, and drop a continuous trail of fish meat from the mongoose's burrow straight across the meadows to the hollow trunk of your banyan tree. The mongooses will follow the trail, enter the hollow, and kill the black cobra!'

Delighted by the advice, the foolish heron purchased fresh carp and laid a trail of fish from the rocks to the banyan tree.

The mongooses smelled the fish, followed the delicious trail eagerly, and arrived at the tree trunk. Entering the hollow burrow, they found the black cobra, fought with savage ferocity, and tore the serpent to shreds, devouring his flesh.

The herons in the branches rejoiced, believing their troubles were over.

Yet once the mongooses had eaten the snake and the fish, they looked up into the branches. Smelling the eggs and young fledglings in the nests, the mongooses climbed the rough bark of the banyan with ease. Day after day, they returned, devouring not only the cobra, but every single heron chick and adult bird on the tree, until the entire colony was wiped out.

Thus Vishnu Sharma warned:
"He who invites a deadlier foe to drive a pest away,
Thinking to solve his grief in haste before the close of day,
Shall find the cure destroy his house and consume his living breed,
Leaving him ruined by the curse of his ill-counseled deed."
moral: Do not invite a greater predator to destroy a lesser pest; the remedy may devour you in the end.

title: The Mice That Ate Iron
summary: In a flourishing merchant town lived a merchant's son named Jeernadhana. Having lost his fortune through misfortune and bad trading, he r...
full_text:
In a flourishing merchant town lived a merchant's son named Jeernadhana. Having lost his fortune through misfortune and bad trading, he resolved to travel to foreign lands to rebuild his wealth. His sole remaining possession of value was a massive, antique balance-scale made of one thousand pounds of solid, tempered iron, inherited from his ancestors.

Before departing, Jeernadhana carried the iron scale to the house of a wealthy neighbor, a merchant named Shreshthi, saying: 'Friend, keep this heavy iron balance safely in your storehouse until I return from my travels.' Shreshthi accepted the scale with pleasant assurances.

Years passed, and through diligence, courage, and honest commerce, Jeernadhana amassed a new fortune and returned to his native city.

Visiting Shreshthi's mansion, he said politely: 'Friend, I have returned. Pray return my ancestral iron scale.'

Shreshthi, who had secretly sold the valuable iron to an armorer for a large sum of gold, made a sorrowful face and sighed: 'Alas, brother! I stored your scale in the dry corner of my grain vault. But a plague of monstrous mice infested the storehouse, and they gnawed through the solid iron and devoured the entire scale! Not an ounce remains!'

Jeernadhana knew well that mice do not eat iron, but concealing his anger, he replied with a gentle smile: 'Do not grieve, friend. If mice have eaten it, it is no fault of yours. The things of this transient world are perishable. Let us put the loss behind us. Today, I am going down to the river to perform my purification bath; send your young son Ramu with me to carry my towel and bath-oil.'

Deceived by Jeernadhana's mild manner, Shreshthi called his beloved only son: 'Go with your uncle, child, and carry his bath-basket.'

Taking the boy to the river, Jeernadhana finished his ablutions. He then led the boy into a deep, secluded limestone cave near the bank, pushed him inside, rolled a colossal boulder across the entrance to seal the cavern, and walked back alone to Shreshthi's house.

Seeing him return without the boy, Shreshthi cried out in alarm: 'Where is my son Ramu? Why did he not return with you from the river?'

Jeernadhana sighed with profound sorrow: 'Alas, friend! As we walked along the riverbank, a colossal mountain hawk swooped down from the clouds, seized your boy by his shoulders in his talons, and carried him away into the sky!'

Shreshthi turned purple with rage: 'Liar! Thief! Murderer! How can a hawk carry away a fifteen-year-old boy? No bird on earth has such strength! Return my son this instant, or I will drag you before the royal magistrates!'

Shreshthi dragged Jeernadhana to the royal court, shouting before the judges: 'This villain has kidnapped and murdered my only son!'

The magistrates reprimanded Jeernadhana: 'Surrender the merchant's son immediately! How can you utter such an absurd falsehood, claiming that a hawk carried away a grown youth?'

Jeernadhana bowed low and replied with calm dignity:
"In a town where hungry mice can eat a thousand pounds of steel,
A hawk can carry off a boy with equal truth and zeal!
If mice can chew through solid iron upon the storehouse floor,
Why marvel that a soaring hawk should take the son next door?"

The chief judge stared in wonder, then burst into hearty laughter: 'Explain this riddle!'

Jeernadhana revealed how Shreshthi had stolen his thousand-pound iron scale under the pretext that mice had eaten it.

The judges ordered Shreshthi to return the iron scale immediately or face the gallows. Weeping in shame, Shreshthi produced the scale, while Jeernadhana rolled back the boulder and restored the boy safe and sound to his father's arms.

Thus Vishnu Sharma taught:
"When deceitful knaves employ absurd and hollow lies,
Answer their foolish falsehoods with an equal, sharp surprise;
For he who claims that mice eat iron must bear the sudden shock
When his own stolen boy is borne aloft by hawk and rock."
moral: Answer deceit with equal wit; he who claims an absurdity must not complain when absurd justice is repaid in kind.

title: The Results of Education
summary: In the high branches of a sacred fig tree on the slopes of the Vindhya mountains, a mother parrot laid two eggs. When the fledglings hatc...
full_text:
In the high branches of a sacred fig tree on the slopes of the Vindhya mountains, a mother parrot laid two eggs. When the fledglings hatched, a fowler climbed the tree and captured them. One brother slipped from the fowler's pouch and tumbled into the tranquil courtyard of a Vedic hermitage, where the sage Agastya and his disciples chanted sacred hymns, recited philosophy, and welcomed weary pilgrims with gentle blessings. The other fledgling was carried to the bustling encampment of ruthless mountain bandits, where he listened day and night to coarse shouting, threats of plunder, and foul curses.

Years passed, and King Jayatsena of Kosala went hunting in the wilderness. Chasing a swift deer, the king became separated from his retinue and rode his lathered horse near the bandits' clearing. Perched on a dead tamarind bough, the second parrot shrieked: 'Look! A rich traveler on a royal stallion! Run, brothers, strike him down, tear off his silk coat, and strip his gold necklace before he escapes!' Hearing the bloodthirsty cries, the startled monarch wheeled his mount and galloped away into the forest.

Presently, the king arrived at the peaceful glade of the hermitage. Cool breezes stirred the lotuses in the crystal pond. On a low sandalwood bough perched the first parrot, who bowed his emerald head and said with melodious grace: 'Welcome, noble traveler! Enter our peaceful hermitage, drink the sweet cool water of our spring, rest your weary limbs in the fragrant shade, and accept the humble fruits of our forest until the revered sage returns.'

Marveling at the contrast between the two birds of identical plumage, the king reflected upon the supreme power of environment and company. Thus Vishnu Sharma taught the princes:
"A ruby cast in filth appears an uninviting stone,
While clay shaped with perfume breathes a fragrance not its own;
So beings take the color of the company they keep,
And from the seeds of association their destinies will reap."
moral: One's character and speech are shaped by company; good association produces virtue, while evil company breeds malice.

title: The Sensible Enemy
summary: In a quiet village lived an impoverished, pious Brahmin named Drona. He had received as a charitable gift a pair of young, healthy calves...
full_text:
In a quiet village lived an impoverished, pious Brahmin named Drona. He had received as a charitable gift a pair of young, healthy calves, which he nourished with gruel and fresh grass until they grew into two magnificent, sleek, fat bullocks.

A thief in the neighboring hamlet observed the fat cattle and thought: 'I will steal those two bullocks tonight and sell them at the fair.'

As the thief was walking down the dark forest trail toward the Brahmin's cottage carrying a stout rope, he encountered a terrifying apparition: a tall, skeletal demon, or Rakshasa, with flaming yellow eyes, sharp fangs projecting from his lips, and a matted beard like dry thatch.

The terrified thief stammered: 'Who are you, lord of darkness?'

The demon replied: 'I am Satyavachana, a flesh-eating demon. I eat only once every three days, and tonight I am walking to the village to devour the pious Brahmin Drona in his bed. Who are you?'

The thief felt his courage return: 'I am a thief! I am going to the same cottage to steal his two fat bullocks! Since our errands lie in the same house, let us go together.'

Reaching the cottage, they crept through the garden gate and slipped into the courtyard. The two fat bullocks were tethered securely beneath the shed, while the exhausted Brahmin slept soundly upon his rope cot on the veranda.

The demon stepped forward, baring his fangs: 'Stand aside, thief! I will devour the Brahmin first while he sleeps!'

The thief seized the demon's arm: 'No! If you attempt to seize the Brahmin, he may awake, scream, and arouse the neighbors! If the villagers rush out with clubs, I will not be able to steal the bullocks! Let me untie the cattle and lead them into the lane first, and then you may devour the Brahmin at your leisure!'

The demon growled in anger: 'If you untie the cattle first, their clattering hooves will awaken the Brahmin! If he wakes, my feast is ruined! I will eat him first!'

'No, I will take the cattle first!' hissed the thief.

Their argument grew heated. In their stubborn pride, they forgot all stealth and began shouting at each other in the courtyard. The demon roared: 'I will eat him now!' while the thief shouted: 'You shall not spoil my theft!'

The loud shouting woke the sleeping Brahmin. Sitting up on his cot, he saw the demon and the thief quarreling before him.

The thief immediately pointed at the demon and yelled: 'Brahmin, beware! This demon has come to devour you!'

The demon shrieked in fury: 'Brahmin, beware! This thief has come to steal your two fat bullocks!'

Realizing his danger, the Brahmin leaped from his cot, seized his heavy iron cudgel, and began reciting his most powerful sacred mantras. Terrified by the holy chants, the demon dissolved into the shadows, while the Brahmin raised his cudgel and chased the thief into the night.

Both the Brahmin's life and his cattle were preserved because his two enemies quarreled between themselves.

Thus Vishnu Sharma taught:
"When enemies dispute the prize and quarrel on the floor,
Their mutual contention drives the peril from the door;
The thief and demon quarreled over who should strike the first,
And left the sleeping Brahmin safe when their alliance burst."
moral: A prudent enemy who argues over terms is safer than a foolish friend who blunders into disaster.

title: The Foolish Friend
summary: In an ancient kingdom ruled a powerful monarch who was passionately fond of unusual pets. Among his royal menagerie was a favorite wild a...
full_text:
In an ancient kingdom ruled a powerful monarch who was passionately fond of unusual pets. Among his royal menagerie was a favorite wild ape that had been trained to perform courtly tricks. The king took such delight in the monkey's agility and amusing antics that he made him his constant companion, allowing him to enter his private apartments and roam freely throughout the palace.

Because the king showered the animal with silks, nuts, and royal favor, the pampered monkey regarded himself as the king's most loyal and devoted guardian.

One sweltering summer afternoon, the king retired to his private bedchamber for his customary siesta. The chamber was cool, scented with sandalwood paste and shaded with vetiver blinds. Desiring undisturbed rest, the king dismissed all his courtiers and sentries, commanding the monkey alone to watch beside his couch and keep off the insects.

The king lay down upon his silk divan and soon fell into a deep, peaceful slumber, breathing rhythmically.

The monkey sat on a velvet footstool, holding a magnificent royal fly-whisk made of yak's tail set with an emerald handle. He watched over his sleeping master with earnest, comical vigilance.

Presently, a persistent bluebottle fly buzzed through the open window, circled the room, and alighted directly upon the king's broad, sleeping chest.

The monkey waved the fly-whisk vigorously: 'Shoo! Away, insolent insect!'

The fly buzzed into the air, circled the bedpost, and settled upon the king's throat.

The monkey waved the whisk again. The fly took wing, danced in the air, and landed squarely upon the king's nose.

Again and again, the monkey drove the insect away, but the persistent fly returned, settling upon the royal forehead, then the ear, and finally right upon the monarch's bare throat.

The monkey's temper flared into uncontrollable fury. 'Insolent wretch!' chattered the enraged animal, grinding his teeth. 'How dare you mock my vigilance and disturb the sleep of my royal master? I will end your buzzing forever!'

Dropping the gentle fly-whisk, the foolish monkey caught sight of the king's sharp, double-edged royal battle-sword resting in its scabbard beside the bed. Drawing the heavy steel blade with both hands, the monkey waited until the fly settled motionless upon the king's chest.

With all his might, the ape brought the razor-sharp sword down upon the fly!

The agile fly took wing and buzzed harmlessly to the ceiling. But the heavy steel blade cleaved through the king's ribs, striking him dead upon his bed!

Hearing the terrible crash, the royal guards rushed into the bedchamber to find their monarch slain by the hand of his most favored pet, who stood over the corpse with the bloody blade, bewildered by his failure to kill the fly.

Thus Vishnu Sharma taught the princes:
"A foolish friend who loves you well, yet lacks all common sense,
Brings swifter ruin to your head than hatred could commence;
Far better is a prudent foe who keeps his distance cold
Than the brainless friend whose clumsy love strikes down your house of gold."
moral: A wise enemy is far better than a foolish friend who harms with the best intentions.

title: The Winning of Friends (Frame)
summary: Revered Vishnu Sharma opened the second scroll of statecraft, Mitra-labha, or The Winning of Friends, before the royal princes: 'Hearken,...
full_text:
Revered Vishnu Sharma opened the second scroll of statecraft, Mitra-labha, or The Winning of Friends, before the royal princes: 'Hearken, noble pupils! Just as false counselors destroy an established alliance, so humble and loyal companions, though lacking wealth and weapons, achieve triumph through united affection. Witness the immortal brotherhood of the Crow, the Mouse, the Turtle, and the Deer.'

In the dense forest of Dandaka stood an ancient, leafy silk-cotton tree where dwelt a wise and observant crow named Laghupatanaka, or Swift. One morning, the crow saw a sinister fowler spread a net of cord upon the forest floor, scatter grains of golden rice across the mesh, and conceal himself behind a cluster of bushes.

Presently, Chitragriva, King of the Pigeons, flew over with his flock. Seeing the rice, the hungry pigeons alighted to eat, and in an instant, every bird was hopelessly entangled in the cords. Chitragriva commanded: 'Do not struggle in divided panic! Let every bird beat his wings together in unison at my count!' The flock beat their wings in perfect harmony, lifted the entire heavy net into the air, and soared above the treetops, leaving the bewildered fowler staring in dismay.

Swift the crow followed their flight in admiration. Chitragriva flew straight to the burrow of his loyal friend, a clever mouse named Hiranyaka, or Gold. Hearing his friend's call, the mouse emerged from his underground fortress and, with his razor-sharp teeth, gnawed through the cords, setting every pigeon free.

Witnessing the mouse's extraordinary loyalty, Swift thought: 'My nature is to eat mice, and his is to fear crows; yet I must win the friendship of this noble soul.' Swift perched outside the burrow, offering solemn vows of brotherhood. Though cautious at first, Hiranyaka recognized the crow's sincere nobility, and they swore an eternal pact of friendship.

Later, the crow carried the mouse on his back to a tranquil, spring-fed lake in the southern hills, introducing him to Mantharaka, an ancient and philosophical water tortoise. The three lived in joyous harmony, sharing meals of sweet seeds and conversing on philosophy.

One afternoon, a panting, terrified spotted deer named Chitranga, or Spot, dashed into their clearing, pursued by royal hunting hounds. Mantharaka slipped into the deep water; Swift flew into the high branches, and Hiranyaka darted into a root-hollow. Observing that no hunters followed, the turtle paddled to the bank and welcomed the panting deer: 'Drink the sweet water, brother, and fear nothing. We offer you our friendship and sanctuary.'

Spot rejoiced, and the four distinct creatures—winged, scaly, four-footed, and burrowing—lived together as devoted brothers. Through their mutual vigilance and quick wits, they later rescued Spot when he fell into a hunter's snare and freed Mantharaka when the hunter bound him in a leather sack, proving forever that genuine friendship conquers every peril of life.

Thus Vishnu Sharma taught:
"Though varied be their species, though differing in their frame,
True friends united in their love protect each other's name;
The crow, the mouse, the tortoise, and the spotted mountain deer,
By brotherhood and loyalty conquered every fear."
moral: Wise and loyal companions, even if physically weak or small, accomplish through mutual aid what mighty armies cannot.

title: The Bharunda Birds
summary: Upon the rugged, wind-swept shores of the Northern Ocean lived a marvelous, mythical bird named Bharunda. This extraordinary creature pos...
full_text:
Upon the rugged, wind-swept shores of the Northern Ocean lived a marvelous, mythical bird named Bharunda. This extraordinary creature possessed two distinct, fully formed heads, each with its own sharp beak, bright eyes, and independent mind, yet both heads were united upon a single neck, growing from a single body with one heart, two wings, and one common stomach.

One sunny afternoon, while walking along the rocky surf, the first head saw a fruit of the celestial nectar-tree fallen from a cliff onto the foam—golden, luscious, and dripping with heavenly sweetness.

Dipping its beak into the foam, the first head seized the fruit and began eating with rapturous delight: 'Oh, what divine nectar! In all my years upon this earth, I have never tasted such intoxicating sweetness! My tongue dances with joy!'

Hearing these ecstatic praises, the second head turned and said eagerly: 'Brother, we share one common frame and one destiny! Give me a share of that miraculous fruit, so that my beak and palate may also savor its celestial sweetness!'

The first head sneered with selfish pride: 'Why should I surrender a morsel to you? Since we share a single stomach, the nourishment from this fruit goes equally into our belly, whether it passes through your throat or mine! The pleasure of chewing belongs to me alone!' With that, the selfish head gulped down the remaining half of the fruit, smacking its beak in triumphant mockery.

The second head burned with silent, resentful fury: 'You have denied me a simple share out of pure spite! You shall soon learn that he who scorns his brother destroys himself!'

A few days later, while foraging among the mountain crags, the second head noticed a shriveled, oily fruit of the deadly poison-nut bush growing in a dark crevice—a fruit whose single drop of venom curdled the blood and rotted the marrow.

Reaching down, the second head seized the poisonous fruit in its beak.

The first head shrieked in horror: 'Madman! Drop that fruit immediately! That is the deadly venom-nut! If you swallow it, we will both perish in agony!'

The vengeful second head laughed with bitter malice: 'Did you not tell me that it matters not which throat the food enters, since both throats feed one stomach? You enjoyed the sweetness of nectar alone; now you shall share the bitterness of death with me!'

Ignoring the frantic pleadings and screams of the first head, the second head swallowed the poisonous fruit whole.

Within seconds, the deadly venom entered the shared bloodstream. Agonizing cramps seized their frame; their single heart stopped beating, their wings collapsed, and the two-headed bird tumbled lifeless upon the rocks, destroyed by its own internal hatred.

Thus Vishnu Sharma taught:
"When those who share a single roof and drink a common bread
Allow the bitter seeds of spite within their house to spread,
The vengeful blow that malice strikes to bring a brother low
Consumes the striker and his home in one destructive blow."
moral: Internal discord and spite between those who share a single body or house leads to the destruction of both.

title: Gold's Gloom
summary: In a quiet monastery near the southern city dwelt a pious ascetic named Chudakarna. Living on the alms of the faithful, he received daily...
full_text:
In a quiet monastery near the southern city dwelt a pious ascetic named Chudakarna. Living on the alms of the faithful, he received daily a clay bowl filled with fine rice, sweets, and lentils. What he could not finish for dinner, he hung in a wicker basket from an iron peg driven high into the ceiling, intending to eat it for breakfast.

In that same hermitage lived a remarkably agile, fat, and daring mouse named Hiranyaka, or Gold. Every night, while the ascetic slept, Gold made an astonishing leap from the stone floor, soaring four cubits into the air to land squarely in the hanging basket. He feasted on the delicious rice, invited his mouse companions to share the spoils, and made a mockery of the hermit's precautions.

Chudakarna was tormented. Night after night, he would lie awake with a split bamboo cane, striking the wooden bedpost with a sharp crack—WHACK!—to frighten the leaping mouse, but the moment his eyelids drooped, Gold leaped and devoured the food.

One evening, an ascetic guest named Brihatsphik arrived from a distant pilgrimage. As they conversed on holy philosophy, Chudakarna absentmindedly struck his cane against the bedpost: WHACK!

Offended, the guest frowned: 'Sir! I speak to you of sacred scriptures, and you answer me by beating the bedpost! Since you hold your guest in such contempt, I shall depart immediately!'

Chudakarna pleaded for pardon: 'Revered brother, forgive me! I do not strike out of disrespect, but because a wretched mouse leaps four cubits into the air to devour the alms in my hanging basket!'

The guest pondered and said: 'No ordinary mouse can leap four cubits into the air! There must be an underlying cause. Just as a man puffed up with vast wealth walks with an arrogant stride, so this mouse possesses some hidden hoard of treasure that fills his heart with supernatural confidence and vigor! Let us discover his underground cache!'

Taking an iron spade, the guest and Chudakarna dug beneath the mud floor of the hermitage. Following the mouse's subterranean tunnels, they broke into a secret cavern where Gold had accumulated thousands of bright gold dinars dropped over decades by careless pilgrims.

'Here is the secret of his leap!' exclaimed the guest, gathering every single gold coin into a heavy leather sack.

When Gold returned to his burrow that evening, he found his treasure cache empty—the shining gold that was his pride was completely gone! A cold gloom settled over his little heart. His legs felt heavy as lead; his bounding energy evaporated, and when he tried to leap toward the hanging basket that night, he could not spring even half a cubit from the floor! He tumbled awkwardly onto his nose, bruised and helpless.

Chudakarna laughed: 'Look at the thief now! Stripped of his gold, he has lost his bounce, his pride, and his companions!'

Abandoning the hermitage, Gold retired to the forest, finding peace in the simple life of a woodland mouse, having learned that wealth breeds restless vanity, while simplicity brings quiet safety.

Thus Vishnu Sharma taught:
"The pride that makes the spirit leap and strut with haughty grace
Resides in piles of hoarded gold within a secret place;
When fortune strips the golden heap that fed the vanity,
The fallen boaster walks the earth with meek humility."
moral: Wealth brings pride and arrogance, while its loss restores humility and peace of mind.

title: Mother Shandilee's Bargain
summary: In a bustling market town lived a frugal housewife named Mother Shandilee. Having gathered a harvest of white sesame seeds, she carefully...
full_text:
In a bustling market town lived a frugal housewife named Mother Shandilee. Having gathered a harvest of white sesame seeds, she carefully hulled them, soaked them in fragrant rosewater, and dried them in the sun, intending to press them into sweet, golden cooking oil for a religious festival.

While the sesame seeds were drying on clean mats in her courtyard, a dirty, mangy dog strayed through the gate and contaminated the seeds with his filthy snout.

Seeing the food defiled for sacred rituals, Mother Shandilee was in despair. She could not use the defiled sesame for temple offerings, yet her thrifty heart could not bear to throw away several bushels of hulled seed.

She devised a cunning barter. Putting the contaminated hulled sesame into a large brass basin, she walked through the village streets shouting: 'Ho, good neighbors! Come and trade! I offer a full basket of clean, hulled, fragrant sesame seeds in exchange for an equal measure of raw, unhulled sesame!'

A simple, gullible neighbor woman ran out with a basket of raw sesame, eager to make the trade: 'What a miraculous bargain! She gives sweet, hulled sesame for cheap, raw seeds!'

As the neighbor was about to hand over her basket, her wise husband emerged from the house. Inspecting Mother Shandilee's eager eyes and the unusual offer, the husband pulled his wife back: 'Hold your hand, foolish woman! In this world, no trader gives pure gold for base copper without a hidden reason! Why would anyone spend hours hulling sesame only to exchange it for raw seed? There is a secret taint, a defilement, or a fraud behind this bargain!'

The husband questioned Mother Shandilee sharply; confused and embarrassed, she admitted that a dog had defiled the grain. The trade was refused, and the neighbor's household was saved from pollution.

Thus Vishnu Sharma taught:
"When unexpected profit calls with sweet, alluring sound,
And bargains that defy all sense upon your path are found,
Pause and examine well the prize before you take the bait,
Lest hidden ruin, rot, and shame within the bargain wait."
moral: When someone offers a bargain that seems too favorable to be true, suspect a hidden flaw or deceit.

title: Self-defeating Forethought
summary: In the city of Kalyanpur lived a miserable, penurious hunter named Bhairava. Though skilled with the bow and successful in his trade, he ...
full_text:
In the city of Kalyanpur lived a miserable, penurious hunter named Bhairava. Though skilled with the bow and successful in his trade, he was so consumed by avarice that he begrudged himself even a handful of parched gram, wearing ragged homespun and hoarding every copper penny he received.

One morning, Bhairava took his heavy composite horn-bow and sharp iron-tipped arrows, setting out into the deep jungle to hunt. He stalked a magnificent, fat spotted deer through the brushwood and brought it down with a clean shot through the heart. Shouldering the heavy carcass, he prepared to turn homeward, overjoyed by his good fortune.

Suddenly, a ferocious, tusked wild boar crossed his path, grunting fiercely. Greed conquered prudence; unwilling to leave the boar behind, the hunter nocked another arrow and shot the beast in the throat. Struck with a mortal wound, the enraged boar charged forward with blinding speed, gored the hunter through his stomach with his razor-sharp tusks, and collapsed dead across the hunter's feet.

At that same moment, a venomous viper disturbed by the struggle struck the boar's snout, dying of the boar's thrashing.

Thus, within a single circle of blood lay four dead bodies: the deer, the wild boar, the hunter, and the serpent!

Presently, a famished, miserly jackal named Dirghamukha wandered into the clearing. Seeing four fat carcasses lying ready for the taking, his little eyes gleamed with ecstasy: 'O divine Fortune! What an inexhaustible mountain of wealth! Here is food to sustain me for three full months!'

Yet his innate, obsessive miserliness asserted itself: 'A prudent beast does not gorge his belly in reckless haste. He eats slowly, saving the best for tomorrow. First, I will eat this thin, tough bowstring made of dried gut; it will satisfy my morning hunger, and I can preserve the succulent meat of the deer, boar, and hunter for future weeks!'

The foolish jackal walked up to the heavy horn-bow lying bent on the turf. He seized the taut, stretched bowstring between his teeth and gnawed on the gut.

The moment his sharp fangs severed the strained cord, the powerful horn-bow uncoiled with the force of an iron catapult. The heavy, sharp-tipped horn end snapped upward like lightning, struck the jackal squarely in the forehead, pierced his brain, and killed him on the spot!

Thus the hoarder died before tasting a single morsel of the vast feast he had hoarded.

Thus Vishnu Sharma taught:
"The hoarder starves his living soul to pile his treasures high,
Denying food and charity beneath the open sky;
Yet sudden fate uncoils its spring before his feast is fed,
And leaves the miser in the dust among his treasures dead."
moral: Extreme stinginess that hoards without enjoyment or charity leads to sudden and ironic loss.

title: Mister Duly
summary: In a holy temple town lived a weaver named Somilaka, whose skill at the loom surpassed all rivals. He wove garments of ethereal beauty, a...
full_text:
In a holy temple town lived a weaver named Somilaka, whose skill at the loom surpassed all rivals. He wove garments of ethereal beauty, adorned with gold thread and floral borders, which fetched enormous prices from princes and nobles. Yet despite his ceaseless labor and large earnings, poverty clung to him like a shadow: whatever gold he earned slipped through his fingers on sudden illnesses, family misfortunes, or taxes, so that he was perpetually in debt.

Other weavers in the same town, who produced coarse, clumsy cloth and worked only three hours a day, lived in two-story brick mansions, wore silks, and dined on delicacies.

Brooding upon this injustice, Somilaka wept: 'Why does fortune mock my honest industry? I will abandon this cursed city and seek wealth in foreign lands!'

Traveling to the distant capital of Vardhamana, he labored for three years and accumulated three hundred gold dinars. Tying the gold in a waistcloth, he set out for home.

Resting for the night under a banyan tree, he was awakened at midnight by two mysterious, glowing celestial figures conversing in the branches.

One figure said: 'Brother Vidhata! Why did you grant three hundred gold dinars to Somilaka? You know well that in his past lives, he performed no charity, and his karma allows him nothing beyond daily food and coarse clothing!'

The second figure replied: 'It is my duty to reward diligence with opportunity, brother; but it is your duty, as Fate, to restrict what he may enjoy.'

When Somilaka woke at dawn, his waistcloth had been untied: a wandering thief had stolen all three hundred gold dinars!

Brokenhearted, the weaver returned to Vardhamana, labored for another three years, and saved another three hundred dinars. On his journey home, he took shelter in a roadside inn, but during the night, a sudden accidental fire broke out, burning his purse to ashes.

Despairing of life, Somilaka climbed a high cliff, resolved to hang himself from a branch.

As he tied the noose, a luminous celestial voice echoed from the sky: 'Hold your hand, Somilaka! I am Fate. It is I who took your hoarded gold, for you have not the karma to hold idle wealth. Yet because of your sincere industry, I grant you a boon: ask for whatever you desire!'

Somilaka replied: 'Grant me wealth!'

The voice asked: 'What would you do with wealth you cannot enjoy?'

Somilaka reflected upon the rich misers who guard gold without peace, and upon the contented poor who sleep without fear. He said: 'Grant me sufficient food, honorable clothing, and a contented heart that accepts what is duly mine!'

The celestial voice blessed him: 'So shall it be, Mister Duly!'

Returning to his loom, Somilaka labored with cheerful peace, receiving always what was sufficient for his honor, free from the torment of greed.

Thus Vishnu Sharma taught:
"What karma has decreed for each by ancient deeds and true,
Will surely reach his open hand in its appointed due;
He who seeks more than he has sown reaps bitterness and pain,
While he who lives with grateful heart finds peace his greatest gain."
moral: What is ordained by one's own past actions will surely come to pass; do not grieve over unavoidable losses.

title: Soft the Weaver
summary: In a quiet village lived a gentle, simple-minded weaver named Mantharaka, known to all as Soft because of his mild and compliant nature. ...
full_text:
In a quiet village lived a gentle, simple-minded weaver named Mantharaka, known to all as Soft because of his mild and compliant nature. One day, while weaving a heavy carpet, the wooden frame of his ancestral loom cracked and splintered beyond repair.

Shouldering his axe, Soft walked into the forest to find a sturdy tree of seasoned timber to hew a new loom-beam. Wandering to the seashore, he found a majestic, ancient shisham tree, tall, straight, and branchless for thirty cubits.

As the weaver raised his iron axe to strike the trunk, a luminous tree spirit emerged from the bark and pleaded: 'Hold your blow, gentle artisan! This ancient tree is my sacred dwelling. If you spare my home, I will grant you any boon your heart desires!'

Soft lowered his axe, bowed politely, and said: 'Revered spirit, I must consult my dear friend and my beloved wife before I choose my wish. Remain here, and I will return shortly.'

Soft hurried to the village and visited his friend, the town barber. Explaining the spirit's offer, Soft asked: 'What should I ask for, brother?'

The barber's eyes gleamed with ambition: 'Ask to be made King of this realm! You can rule from a golden palace, and make me your grand vizier!'

Soft replied: 'Kingship is a burden of endless wars, conspiracies, and sleepless nights. Let me consult my wife; women have great wisdom in domestic affairs.'

The barber warned: 'Never consult a woman on great matters! Women think only of petty vanities!'

Yet Soft returned home and asked his wife: 'Dearest, the tree spirit has granted me a wish. The barber advises me to ask for a kingdom. What is your counsel?'

The wife scoffed: 'A kingdom? Kings are assassinated by their brothers or overthrown by rebellions! Ask for something practical for your trade! You are a weaver with only two hands and one head; ask for another head and two more hands! With four hands and two heads, you can operate two looms simultaneously, weave twice as many carpets, earn double profits, and become the richest merchant in the province without the perils of a crown!'

Pleased by her advice, Soft ran back to the forest and called out: 'O Tree Spirit! Grant me two heads and four hands, so that I may weave with double speed!'

'Your wish is granted!' spoke the spirit.

Instantly, a second head sprouted from Soft's neck, and two additional muscular arms grew from his shoulders!

Rejoicing, Soft marched proudly back into the village to display his marvelous new body to his neighbors.

As he entered the village square, the terrified villagers mistook the four-armed, two-headed apparition for a demonic Rakshasa invading their homes. Crying: 'A monster! A demon has entered the town!' they rushed upon him with iron bars, heavy stones, and clubs, beating poor Soft to death on the spot.

Thus Vishnu Sharma taught:
"He who takes counsel of a fool to shape his fortune's choice,
Ignoring reason, prudence, and the wise preceptor's voice,
Shall find the granted wish transform to ruin in a breath,
And bring the double-headed fool to an untimely death."
moral: Do not consult foolish or greedy advisers when a great opportunity is placed in your hands.

title: Hang-Ball and Greedy
summary: In a rugged wilderness lived a foolish, short-sighted jackal named Mahachatura, accompanied by his hungry mate, Greedy. While trotting th...
full_text:
In a rugged wilderness lived a foolish, short-sighted jackal named Mahachatura, accompanied by his hungry mate, Greedy. While trotting through a thorny scrubland, they saw a massive, long-horned domestic bull belonging to a merchant's caravan, which had strayed into the brush. As the bull walked with heavy, ponderous strides, a pair of large, fleshy dewlaps hung swaying between his hind legs.

Seeing the swaying flesh, the jackal's eyes widened with voracious anticipation: 'Look, wife! Look at that juicy, plump piece of meat dangling from that beast! It is so loosely attached that with the next step, it will surely drop to the earth!'

The jackal's mate, who had better sense, cautioned him: 'Husband, that is part of the living animal's body; it will not drop off. Let us stalk a hare or dig for beetles in the ravine.'

The jackal snapped in annoyance: 'You understand nothing of anatomy! See how it swings back and forth? It will fall within twenty paces! Follow that bull, and we shall feast without the toil of hunting!'

For seven long, exhausting days and nights, the foolish jackal followed the plodding bull through burning ravines, dense thorn bushes, and stony riverbeds. Whenever the bull stopped to graze, the jackal crouched behind a boulder, licking his lips, muttering: 'Now it falls! Now it drops!'

Whenever the bull moved forward, the flesh swayed as before, firmly attached to the beast's frame.

On the eighth day, having eaten nothing and dying of parched exhaustion, the jackal staggered through the brush. The bull, annoyed by the persistent scavenger hovering behind his heels, suddenly kicked backward with his iron-hard hoof, striking the jackal squarely in the ribs, breaking three bones and hurling him into a thorny cactus bush.

Lying bruised and starving among the thorns, the jackal groaned in agony:
"He who pursues an empty hope that swings before his eyes,
Ignoring present certainty to chase an idle prize,
Shall follow weary trails in vain until his bones are sore,
And find an iron hoof of pain repay his folly sore."
moral: Pursuing illusory or impossible hopes while neglecting immediate security leads to bitter disappointment.

title: The Mice That Set Elephant Free
summary: Near the shores of a sparkling mountain lake in the Dandaka forest lay an ancient, ruined city of stone whose marble pavilions and terrac...
keywords: the mice that set elephant free
full_text:
Near the shores of a sparkling mountain lake in the Dandaka forest lay an ancient, ruined city of stone whose marble pavilions and terraces were inhabited by an enormous colony of thousands of wild mice, governed by their king, Hiranyagarbha. The mice lived in peace, raising their families in the mossy crevices and hollow flagstones of the ruins.

One severe summer, the rivers dried up, and an enormous herd of wild forest elephants, led by their majestic patriarch, King Gajendra, marched through the ruins to reach the deep lake.

As the colossal beasts thundered across the stone courtyards, their massive, pillar-like feet trampled upon the subterranean burrows, crushing thousands of mice, shattering nests, and breaking the limbs of many more.

The mice gathered in weeping despair. King Hiranyagarbha said: 'If the elephant herd returns by this same trail, our entire race will be exterminated! Let us petition their noble king.'

Selecting an embassy of elder mice, Hiranyagarbha led them to the lake shore. Standing upon a high mossy boulder, the mouse king bowed to King Gajendra and spoke with dignified eloquence: 'O mighty Monarch of the Forest! As your herd marched through our ancient city, your colossal feet trampled our homes and killed thousands of our children. We come not in anger, but in humble prayer: deign to lead your herd by another trail around the ridge when you return to the hills. If you grant us this mercy, we pledge that if ever your majesty falls into distress, we humble mice will come to your aid!'

The great elephant king looked down upon the tiny mouse. Though he smiled at the idea that tiny mice could ever assist a mountain-crushing elephant, he was moved by their dignity and respect. 'Fear not, little friends,' trumpeted Gajendra kindly. 'I will lead my herd along the valley trail and never disturb your city again.'

Months passed, and the King of the realm sent royal trappers into the forest to capture wild war-elephants. Digging concealed pits and driving the herd with torches, the hunters trapped King Gajendra and bound him with thick, heavy cables of braided leather and steel chains to stout sal trees, intending to starve him into submission.

Tied to the trees, unable to move a limb, Gajendra trumpeted in despair. Suddenly, he remembered the promise of the humble mouse king: 'A drowning man clutches at a straw; let me call my little friends!'

The elephant trumpeted the special distress call that Hiranyagarbha had taught him.

Hearing the call echoing from the hills, the mouse king mobilized his army: millions of mice marched through the forest underbrush. Arriving at the clearing, they swarmed over the heavy leather cables. With millions of sharp, needle-like teeth, the mice gnawed simultaneously through the thick cords and severed the leather lashings!

Within an hour, every cable was sliced to threads, and the colossal elephant was completely free!

King Gajendra lifted the mouse king gently upon his broad forehead in gratitude, trumpeting in wonder:
"Let no colossus mock the weak who crawl upon the floor;
For friendship knows no size or scale upon life's shifting shore;
The mighty beast who bowed his pride to hear the humble plea
Was saved from chains and slavery to wander wild and free."
moral: Never despise the weak or small; the humble mouse may one day break the chains of the mighty elephant.

title: Spot's Captivity
summary: The four devoted companions—Swift the crow, Gold the mouse, Shell-Neck the turtle, and Spot the spotted deer—lived in idyllic peace by th...
full_text:
The four devoted companions—Swift the crow, Gold the mouse, Shell-Neck the turtle, and Spot the spotted deer—lived in idyllic peace by the lily lake. Every evening, they gathered on the grassy bank to share their experiences and rejoice in their brotherhood.

One evening, Spot did not return from his grazing. As the shadows lengthened and twilight turned to night, the three friends grew anxious. 'A hunter must have snared him, or a leopard crossed his trail,' wept Shell-Neck.

Swift the crow said: 'I have wings; I will search the forest from above.' Soaring over the canopy, the crow scanned the clearings in the moonlight. In a secluded bamboo glade, he spotted poor Chitranga, trapped in a hunter's stout mesh of twisted sinew, struggling in vain.

Swift alighted upon a branch: 'Brother Spot! How came you into this snare?'

'Alas, friend!' wept the deer. 'In my haste to reach our meeting, I failed to see the concealed trap. The hunter will return at dawn to slaughter me!'

Swift flew straight back to the lake, took Gold the mouse upon his back, and flew like the wind back to the glade. Gold immediately set to work with his razor teeth, gnawing through the tough sinew knots.

Just as the last cord was severed, Shell-Neck the slow water tortoise arrived, having paddled through the grass out of pure affection for his friend.

Spot cried in alarm: 'Brother Shell-Neck, why did you come? If the hunter arrives, Gold can dart into a hole, Swift can fly into the sky, and I can bound across the clearing, but your slow legs cannot escape!'

At that very moment, the hunter strode into the clearing carrying an iron bow and spear.

Spot leaped away into the thickets; Swift flew into a tall oak, and Gold darted into a root-hollow. Shell-Neck, crawling with all his might, could not reach the water. The hunter, furious at finding his valuable deer escaped, saw the fat tortoise on the grass. 'A tortoise is better than nothing!' he grunted, binding Shell-Neck tightly in his leather game-bag and slinging it across his shoulder.

The three escaped friends were in despair: 'Our beloved brother is carried away to be slaughtered!'

Gold the mouse devised a brilliant rescue plan: 'Swift, fly ahead and alight upon the riverbank in the hunter's path. Spot, run ahead, collapse upon the turf beside the water, and feign death with your limbs stiff and eyes half-closed. Swift, perch upon his head and pretend to peck at his eyes. Seeing a dead deer lying ready, the greedy hunter will drop his heavy sack to seize the deer!'

The companions executed the plan with flawless precision.

As the hunter walked along the riverbank, he saw a magnificent spotted deer lying apparently dead upon the turf, with a crow pecking at its face. Overjoyed, he dropped the heavy game-bag containing Shell-Neck and ran with his knife to claim the carcass.

The instant the hunter stepped away from the bag, Gold the mouse darted from the grass, gnawed through the leather strings, and Shell-Neck slipped into the deep, cool water of the river!

Just as the hunter reached out his hand to seize the deer, Spot sprang to his feet with an agile bound and vanished into the forest, while the crow flew into the trees, cawing in derision.

Bewildered, the hunter returned to pick up his sack, only to find the cord severed and his tortoise gone! Terrified, believing the forest was enchanted by spirits, the hunter fled for his life, never to return.

The four loyal companions reunited at the lake, embracing with tears of joy, having saved each other through selfless love and coordinated courage.

Thus Vishnu Sharma concluded Book 2:
"When friends stand firm in loyalty, united heart and mind,
No snare of cruel circumstance can keep their love confined;
Each brings his strength, each shares the risk, and in the darkest hour,
Their brotherhood breaks every chain with triumphant, noble power."
moral: True friendship is proved in danger; when companions act in concert, each offering his unique strength, no snare can hold them.
