title: Crows and Owls (Frame)
summary: Revered Vishnu Sharma opened the third scroll of wisdom: Kakolukiyam, the classic treatise on War and Peace, Crows and Owls. 'Hearken wel...
full_text:
Revered Vishnu Sharma opened the third scroll of wisdom: Kakolukiyam, the classic treatise on War and Peace, Crows and Owls. 'Hearken well, princes,' spoke the master. 'He who grants shelter to a former enemy, believing flattering words of reconciliation, harbors a flame within his thatch that will consume him in his sleep.'

Near the city of Mahilaropya stood a colossal, ancient banyan tree with thousands of branches, inhabited by a vast flock of crows governed by their wise king, Meghavarna, or Cloud-Color. In a mountain cavern in the neighboring rocky ridges lived an equally vast host of ferocious horned owls, commanded by their sovereign, Arimardana, or Foe-Crusher.

Between crows and owls there existed an ancient, ancestral enmity. Every night, while the crows were blinded by the darkness and slept peacefully in their banyan tree, the owls, possessing night-vision, swooped from the sky, slaughtered hundreds of helpless crows, and returned to their cave with blood-stained talons. The banyan tree was littered with feathers and broken bones.

Desperate to end the slaughter, King Cloud-Color summoned his five chief ministers: Ujjivi, Sanjivi, Anujivi, Prajivi, and his prime minister, the ancient and profound scholar Sthirajiwi, or Long-Lived.

The king asked: 'What shall we do against an enemy who strikes by night when we cannot see, and whose fortress is impregnable by day?'

The first four ministers gave conflicting counsel: some advised submission and tribute; some advised flight to distant mountains; some advised seeking foreign allies.

Long-Lived, the fifth minister, said: 'Neither cowardice nor open battle can save us. We must employ the sixth expedient of statecraft: Dvaidhabhava, the art of strategic deception and espionage. I will allow myself to be plucked of my feathers, bruised, and cast out at the foot of our tree. You, my king, must lead the flock to temporary refuge in the southern mountains, leaving me behind.'

The crows obeyed. They pecked Long-Lived, tore out his feathers, smeared him with blood, and threw him into the dust beneath the tree before departing.

When the owls arrived that night to slaughter the crows, they found the tree empty, except for the bleeding minister groaning upon the ground.

Foe-Crusher's counselors debated whether to kill him. A wise owl named Raktaksha, or Red-Eye, warned: 'Kill this crow immediately! He is the chief counselor of the crow king! A wounded enemy is doubly dangerous, and to spare him is madness!'

Yet the other foolish owl ministers, swayed by Long-Lived's flattering praises of the owl king's majesty and his false curses against his own king, convinced Foe-Crusher to spare him and carry him to their mountain cave as an honored guest.

For weeks, Long-Lived lived at the entrance of the owl cave. Every day, while the owls slept through the daylight hours, he gathered dry twigs, pine needles, and dead brushwood, stacking them innocently around the mouth of the cavern, pretending he was building a warm nest for his featherless body.

When the brushwood pile reached the roof of the cave, Long-Lived flew to his king, Cloud-Color, and summoned the flock. Every crow carried a smoldering twig from a woodcutter's fire. They dropped the burning embers into the dry brushwood, fanning the blaze with their wings.

The dry timber exploded into an inferno. Trapped in the dark, smoky cavern, blinded by the daytime light, the entire army of owls, including their foolish king, perished in the flames and smoke, without a single crow losing a feather!

Long-Lived was hailed as the savior of his race, having conquered through patient espionage what an army could never achieve.

Thus Vishnu Sharma taught:
"He who receives a former foe inside his fortress gate,
Believing tears of penitence and flattery of late,
Builds his own pyre with his hand, and sleeps in foolish trust,
Until the spark of vengeance turns his fortress into dust."
moral: Do not trust a reconciled enemy who lived in your camp; internal espionage destroys the strongest fortress.

title: How the Birds Picked a King
summary: In the golden Age of Truth, the birds of all species assembled upon a vast plateau to select a supreme monarch to govern the feathered ki...
keywords: how the birds picked a king
full_text:
In the golden Age of Truth, the birds of all species assembled upon a vast plateau to select a supreme monarch to govern the feathered kingdom. Swans, peacocks, herons, eagles, parrots, and cuckoos debated long, observing that while four-footed beasts had the lion and aquatic creatures had the great carp, birds lived in disorder without a sovereign.

Noticing a majestic horned owl perched in a nearby hollow, looking solemn and formidable with his great yellow eyes and hooked beak, the assembly cried in unison: 'Behold the Owl! He has an imposing countenance and a grave demeanor! Let us anoint the Owl as King of the Birds!'

Preparations for the coronation were made with immense splendor. Sacred waters from holy rivers were gathered in golden flagons; cushions of silk were laid upon the stone throne, and auspicious hymns were recited by parrots.

Just as the crown of jewels was about to be placed upon the owl's head, an old crow arrived from the northern forest, inquiring: 'What grand festival is this?'

The birds replied: 'We are crowning the Owl as Sovereign of all Birds!'

The crow burst into mocking laughter: 'Are you completely devoid of intellect? Why crown an owl when the majestic Eagle, the peacock, and the royal swan grace our skies? Look at his hideous, hooked beak, his crooked neck, and his terrifying yellow eyes! If he looks so dreadful in peace, how will he appear when enraged? Moreover, he is completely blind by daylight! How can a sovereign protect his subjects when he cannot see the sun? To crown a blind, ill-omened nocturnal predator is to invite destruction!'

Hearing the crow's logical arguments, the assembly was swayed. One by one, the birds dispersed into the sky, leaving the coronation abandoned.

The owl, who had been sitting patiently awaiting the crown, opened his great eyes and asked his servant: 'Why has the music stopped? Where are my subjects?'

The servant replied: 'A single crow spoke against you, and the assembly has dispersed!'

The enraged owl rose upon his rock and cursed the crow with bitter hatred: 'Insolent bird! You have ruined my royal coronation! From this day forward, let there be eternal, mortal enmity between my race and yours!'

With that, the owl flew into the shadows, establishing the ancestral war between crows and owls.

Thus Vishnu Sharma taught:
"A thoughtless tongue that utters scorn and ruins another's pride,
Awakens sleeping hatred that will never be denied;
From that one day upon the hill where mocking words were cast,
The war of crows and owls has raged while centuries have passed."
moral: An ancestral grudge is born of a single tactless insult; choose leaders of noble and gentle character.

title: How the Rabbit Fooled the Elephant
summary: In the great forest of Dandaka lived an enormous herd of wild elephants governed by a colossal tusker named Chaturdanta. A severe, twelve...
keywords: how the rabbit fooled the elephant
full_text:
In the great forest of Dandaka lived an enormous herd of wild elephants governed by a colossal tusker named Chaturdanta. A severe, twelve-year drought dried up all the forest watering holes; the mud cracked, and the great beasts suffered from intolerable thirst.

The elephant king sent scouts to every compass point. One scout returned, reporting that deep within a mountain valley lay a vast, crystal-clear, sacred lake called Chandrasaras, or the Lake of the Moon, fed by subterranean glacial springs.

The elephant herd thundered toward the lake. Surrounding the water were thousands of underground burrows inhabited by a peaceful colony of wild hares. As the thirsty colossi dashed toward the water, their massive feet crushed thousands of burrows, killing and maiming countless hares.

The surviving hares gathered in grief. Their leader, a wise old hare named Vijaya, said: 'If the elephant herd returns daily to drink, our species will be extinguished. I will go as an ambassador and drive them away through intellect.'

Vijaya hopped to the edge of the lake and climbed to the summit of a high, steep granite boulder overlooking the water, out of reach of the elephants' trunks.

When King Chaturdanta strode toward the lake at twilight, the little hare called down in a solemn, ringing voice: 'Halt, King of Elephants! Do not step into these waters!'

The giant stopped in surprise: 'Who are you to command the Sovereign of the Forest?'

Vijaya replied with dignified authority: 'I am Vijaya, the accredited ambassador of the glorious Moon God! The sacred Moon has sent me with this dispatch: "These waters are my holy sanctuary, and the hares who dwell upon these shores are my beloved, sacred children! You have trampled their homes and defiled my lake! If you touch these waters again, I will withdraw my cooling light, parch your herd with fever, and destroy you with my wrath!"'

The elephant king was troubled: 'Where is your royal master, the Moon?'

'He sits upon his liquid throne within this very lake!' said the hare. 'Look down into the water, and behold his divine majesty!'

Chaturdanta stepped to the edge and looked down. The full moon was shining in the cloudless sky, and its perfect, glowing silver disc was mirrored upon the tranquil surface of the water.

Chaturdanta lowered his trunk into the pool to make an oblation of reverence. As his trunk stirred the water, ripples spread across the surface, causing the mirrored moon to tremble, shake, and dance wildly in waves!

'Behold!' cried the clever hare in terror. 'The Moon God trembles with fury because you have disturbed his sacred waters! Prostrate your head in the dust, beg for his divine mercy, and lead your herd away instantly before his wrath consumes you!'

Terrified by the divine omen, the colossal elephant bowed his head to the earth, begged the dancing moon for forgiveness, and led his vast herd away into distant mountains, never to return.

The hares rejoiced, celebrating their clever ambassador who saved their city with pure wit.

Thus Vishnu Sharma taught:
"The weak ambassador who speaks with firm, courageous grace,
Invoking sacred majesty within the danger's place,
Can make the mountain-crushing giant in trembling terror bow,
And turn the mighty army back without an arrow's blow."
moral: A small and weak ambassador who uses sacred authority and psychological wit can turn away an army of giants.

title: The Cat's Judgment
summary: In the hollow of an ancient banyan tree lived a gentle wild francolin partridge named Kapinjala. In a burrow beneath the roots of the sam...
full_text:
In the hollow of an ancient banyan tree lived a gentle wild francolin partridge named Kapinjala. In a burrow beneath the roots of the same tree lived a lively hare named Shighraga. For years they lived as peaceful neighbors.

One day, Kapinjala flew away to distant rice fields where a rich harvest was underway, remaining there for several weeks to feast.

Believing the partridge had perished or abandoned his dwelling, the hare Shighraga moved into the hollow and made it his home.

When Kapinjala returned, he found the hare occupying his ancestral hollow: 'This is my home, hare! Step out immediately!'

The hare refused: 'A hollow belongs to whoever occupies it! Lands, houses, and wells are held by possession, not ancient claims! If you dispute my right, let us seek an arbitrator learned in the law of scriptures.'

As they walked along the riverbank seeking a judge, they saw sitting upon a sandy spit a large, sleek tomcat named Dadhikarna. The cat stood upon one hind leg, facing the rising sun with closed eyes, holding a rosary of tulsi beads in his paw, whispering pious prayers and shedding tears of feigned spiritual ecstasy.

Seeing the holy cat, the partridge whispered: 'Look at that devout ascetic! He has renounced all violence and lives only on wild roots! Let us ask him to judge our dispute!'

The hare was suspicious: 'Cats are our natural mortal enemies! Let us keep our distance!'

Standing thirty paces away, the two disputants called out: 'O holy ascetic! We have a dispute over property. Deign to hear our cause and judge between us according to the sacred law!'

The cat opened his pious eyes, smiled with saintly gentleness, and murmured in a weak, trembling voice: 'Alas, my children! Age has dimmed my eyes and dulled my hearing, and I have renounced the vanities of this world. Yet to maintain justice is a holy duty. Come closer, my children, step right beside my ear and state your cause, so that my aged ears may hear the truth without error.'

Deceived by his holy appearance and feeble voice, the foolish partridge and the simple hare stepped directly between the cat's front paws.

In an instant, the 'holy ascetic' sprang with razor claws: with one paw he seized the partridge, with the other he crushed the hare, and within minutes, he devoured both disputants, settling their legal quarrel forever!

Thus Vishnu Sharma warned:
"He who invites a predator to judge his petty strife,
Believing outer piety and holy forms of life,
Shall find the hypocrite's sharp fangs resolve the legal case,
By swallowing both disputants within his greedy place."
moral: Never select a natural predator as an arbitrator of your dispute, for he will settle the quarrel by devouring both.

title: The Brahmin's Goat
summary: In a quiet village lived a pious, scholarly Brahmin named Mitra Sarman. Having performed a domestic sacrifice for a wealthy patron, he wa...
full_text:
In a quiet village lived a pious, scholarly Brahmin named Mitra Sarman. Having performed a domestic sacrifice for a wealthy patron, he was rewarded with a plump, young, healthy white goat to offer in his ancestral rites. Delighted with his fee, the Brahmin slung the young goat across his shoulders, holding its legs with his hands, and set out along the dusty country road toward his home.

Now on that road dwelt three cunning, unscrupulous rogues who had not eaten meat in days. Seeing the fat goat upon the Brahmin's shoulders, their mouths watered.

The first crook said: 'How can we secure that fat goat without fighting? The Brahmin carries an iron cudgel.'

The second rogue smiled: 'Brute force is unnecessary. If three men tell the same lie with confidence, even a scholar will doubt his own eyes!'

The three rogues separated, stationing themselves along the road at intervals of half a mile.

As the Brahmin walked along, the first rogue approached him, bowing with exaggerated reverence: 'Greetings, revered pandit! But tell me, why does a holy scholar of the Vedas carry an unclean, filthy black dog upon his shoulders? Are you not ashamed of defiling your sacred thread?'

The Brahmin was indignant: 'Are you blind, fool? This is a pure, sacrificial white goat, not an unclean dog! Begone with your madness!'

Shrugging with feigned bewilderment, the first rogue walked on.

The Brahmin continued for another half mile, slightly perplexed.

Presently, the second rogue stepped from behind a tamarind tree and cried out in feigned shock: 'A curse upon this dark age! A pious Brahmin walking the public highway carrying a dead calf upon his back! Have you lost your senses, master?'

The Brahmin stopped, looked at the beast, felt its horns and soft fur, and shouted: 'What is the matter with the people of this district? This is a living goat! Can you not see its horns?'

The second rogue shook his head with pity: 'If you choose to call a dead calf a goat, do so, but do not touch the temple gates!'

Now a gnawing seed of doubt took root in the Brahmin's mind: 'Can this truly be an unclean beast? Could a demon have bewitched my eyes?'

He walked on with heavy, hesitant steps.

After another half mile, the third rogue emerged from the brushwood and exclaimed in horror: 'Revered sir! Step away from me! Why are you carrying a foul, mangy hyena upon your shoulders? Throw down that abomination before its bite poisons you!'

The Brahmin was completely unhinged by the third confirmation. Convinced that the creature upon his shoulders was a shape-shifting demon that appeared as a goat to him, but as a dog, calf, and hyena to others, he threw the goat onto the road in horror and ran for his life toward his village without looking back!

The three laughing rogues caught the fat goat, roasted it over a savory fire, and feasted till dawn.

Thus Vishnu Sharma taught:
"When cunning rogues in concert speak an orchestrated lie,
Repeating falsehood boldly beneath the open sky,
Even the scholar doubts his eyes, surrenders up his prize,
And flees the phantom demon that his foolish fear supplies."
moral: Do not let the repeated assertions of rogues overcome the evidence of your own senses.

title: The Snake and the Ants
summary: In a secluded rocky wasteland lived a monstrous, thick-bodied black serpent named Mandavishya, possessing venom so concentrated that a si...
full_text:
In a secluded rocky wasteland lived a monstrous, thick-bodied black serpent named Mandavishya, possessing venom so concentrated that a single drop could wither a sapling. Proud of his deadly poison and massive coils, the snake terrorized the surrounding scrub, striking down birds, squirrels, and lizards without mercy.

One hot afternoon, the serpent glided across a dry clay ridge and came upon a towering anthill constructed by millions of tiny, industrious black ants. The ants were marching in orderly columns, carrying seeds and bits of leaves into their subterranean galleries.

Arrogant in his colossal size, the serpent coiled himself squarely across their main highway, hissing with contempt: 'Insolent insects! How dare you build your dirt heap in my hunting grounds? Clear your columns from my path, or I will crush your ant-hill to powder!'

The ant elders pleaded politely: 'Mighty serpent, we harm no one; we labor only to store food against the rains. Pray move your heavy tail three paces aside, so our workers may pass.'

Enraged by what he considered impertinence, the snake lashed his heavy tail across the anthill, smashing their earthen arches, crushing thousands of workers, and scattering their larvae into the dust.

In that instant, the call to battle sounded through the subterranean galleries. Millions of tiny black ants swarmed from the depths like a living dark flood!

They did not flee; they did not panic. In an overwhelming, disciplined host, they poured over the serpent's scaly coils. Tens of thousands of tiny ants clamped their microscopic, needle-sharp mandibles simultaneously into the soft flesh between the serpent's scales, biting his eyes, his nostrils, his tongue, and his tender underbelly!

The colossal serpent writhed in agony. He hissed and struck with his fangs, but his venom was useless against millions of tiny adversaries; he lashed his tail, but for every hundred ants crushed, a hundred thousand more clamped their jaws into his skin!

Rolling across the rocks, thrashing in blinded frenzy, the monstrous predator was overwhelmed by the united multitude. Within hours, the giant snake succumbed to the millions of microscopic stings, his colossal carcass stripped to clean white bones.

Thus Vishnu Sharma taught:
"Let no proud tyrant boast his fangs, his venom, or his weight;
For tiny ants when bound in love decide the tyrant's fate;
A single thread of grass may break before the lightest breeze,
Yet woven into cords of strength, it binds the stormy seas."
moral: Even the most colossal and venomous monster is overcome when tiny creatures unite in countless numbers.

title: The Snake Who Paid Cash
summary: In a quiet village lived an impoverished, hardworking farmer named Haridatta. Despite toiling from dawn till dusk under the blazing sun, ...
full_text:
In a quiet village lived an impoverished, hardworking farmer named Haridatta. Despite toiling from dawn till dusk under the blazing sun, his rocky fields yielded meager harvests, and his family lived on parched grain.

One sweltering noon, exhausted by labor, Haridatta lay down to rest beneath the shade of an ancient tree near his field. Looking toward a nearby termite mound, he saw a majestic, enormous black cobra emerging from a burrow, expanding its magnificent hood in the gentle breeze.

Reflecting with reverence, the farmer thought: 'Surely this serpent is the sacred guardian deity of this field! Because I have never offered him oblations, my land has remained barren!'

Hurrying to his hut, he brought a clay saucer filled with fresh, warm cow's milk and placed it respectfully before the mound, praying: 'O Lord of the Earth! Forgive my past neglect, and accept this humble offering.'

Next morning, when Haridatta returned to inspect the saucer, the milk had been drunk, and lying in the center of the clay plate was a shining, pure gold dinar!

Delighted, the farmer took the coin, purchased grain for his family, and placed another saucer of milk. Every morning without fail, the serpent drank the milk and left behind a pure gold coin. Within a year, Haridatta grew prosperous, respected, and free from want.

One season, Haridatta had to travel to a distant city for a week. He instructed his grown son: 'Every evening, place a saucer of milk before the serpent's mound, and retrieve the gold coin in the morning.'

The son placed the milk that evening and found the gold dinar at dawn. But looking at the coin, a dark, greedy thought seized the foolish youth's mind: 'This anthill must be filled with thousands of gold dinars! Why should I wait day by day for a single coin? I will kill this serpent, dig up his mound, and take all his gold at once!'

Arming himself with a heavy iron cudgel, the foolish youth walked to the mound that evening. As the cobra emerged to drink the milk, the boy struck with all his might at the serpent's head!

The blow missed the snake's skull, striking his coils. Enraged by the treacherous attack, the venomous cobra struck with lightning speed, sinking his deadly fangs deep into the youth's ankle!

The deadly venom raced through the boy's veins; he collapsed to the earth and died before he could crawl three paces.

When Haridatta returned from his journey, he found his son a corpse on the funeral pyre. Weeping bitter tears over his son's foolish greed, the farmer took a bowl of milk and walked to the mound, hoping to restore the old compact.

The cobra emerged, but remained coiled at a safe distance on the rocks: 'Haridatta! You come out of greed, while I remember the blow of your son's cudgel. The bond between us is broken forever. You cannot forget the pyre of your son, and I cannot forget my bruised coils. Depart, and return no more!'

With that, the serpent retreated into the depths of the earth, leaving Haridatta in poverty and grief.

Thus Vishnu Sharma taught:
"The golden fountain flows with grace for him who takes his share;
But he who strikes with greedy hand to strip the treasure bare,
Destroys the source of all his wealth, and reaps in bitter grief
The deadly fruit that sudden haste bestows upon the thief."
moral: Greed that seeks to seize everything in a single day destroys the golden fountain of daily blessing.

title: The Unsocial Swans
summary: In a lush royal valley lay a magnificent lake whose waters were carpeted with golden lotuses and crystal water-lilies. Inhabiting this pa...
full_text:
In a lush royal valley lay a magnificent lake whose waters were carpeted with golden lotuses and crystal water-lilies. Inhabiting this paradise was a large flock of haughty, unsocial wild swans whose feathers gleamed like polished silver. Every six months, by royal decree, the swans dropped a single golden feather from their plumage upon the marble pavilion as tribute to the King of the realm, who in return protected the lake from all hunters.

Proud of their royal privilege and their golden feathers, the swans grew excessively arrogant, considering the lake their exclusive property.

One afternoon, a magnificent wild bird of another species—a grand, golden-crested gander with broad wings and noble manners—arrived from distant northern mountains. Alighting upon the water, he bowed politely to the flock: 'Greetings, noble swans! I have traveled far over the snowy peaks; permit me to rest in this tranquil lake, and I will share with you the wisdom of foreign lands.'

The swans hissed with indignant pride: 'Depart from this water immediately, insolent intruder! This lake was granted exclusively to our flock by the King! Every six months we pay rent with our golden feathers! How dare you settle here without paying tribute? Depart, or we will peck your eyes out!'

The noble gander pleaded for simple hospitality, but the arrogant swans attacked him in a swarm, beating him with their wings and driving him from the water.

Stung by their cruelty, the gander flew straight to the King's palace, alighting before the open marble council hall. Bowing low, he spoke with eloquence: 'O Sovereign of the Earth! I arrived as a peaceful guest at your lotus lake, but your swans attacked me with savage fury, shouting: "What care we for the King? This lake is ours, and the King is nothing but our tenant who begs for our shed feathers!"'

The King was furious at this reported insolence. He summoned his royal huntsmen: 'Go to the lotus lake immediately! Slaughter those arrogant swans, and bring their carcasses to the royal kitchen!'

Hearing the blare of the royal hunting horns and seeing the fowlers marching with arrows and nets, the terrified swans abandoned their golden lotuses and took to the sky in frantic panic, fleeing the kingdom forever, homeless and destitute.

Thus Vishnu Sharma taught:
"He who denies the stranger rest and drives the guest away,
Boasting of royal privilege and wealth from day to day,
Shall see his arrogance provoke the monarch's iron hand,
And flee in terror from the home he thought his sovereign land."
moral: Arrogance that drives away peaceful guests invites the wrath of the sovereign.

title: The Self-sacrificing Dove
summary: A cruel and ruthless fowler spent his life wandering the forests with nets and lime-twigs, capturing songbirds, tearing their wings, and ...
full_text:
A cruel and ruthless fowler spent his life wandering the forests with nets and lime-twigs, capturing songbirds, tearing their wings, and selling them to slaughterhouses. He knew neither pity nor piety.

One freezing evening, a violent winter tempest broke over the wilderness. Freezing rain fell in torrents; howling winds stripped the trees, and the forest grew black as pitch. Shivering with cold, his teeth chattering, his fingers numb, the fowler sought shelter beneath the spreading boughs of an ancient fig tree. He had captured a gentle wild female dove earlier that afternoon, keeping her shivering inside his wicker cage.

In the high branches of that very tree sat the male dove, weeping for his absent mate: 'Alas! The tempest rages and night has fallen, yet my beloved has not returned. Without her, this empty nest is a barren desert!'

Hearing his voice, the captured dove called from the wicker cage below: 'Husband, grieve not for me! Behold, beneath our tree sits a human guest, shivering and dying of the freezing cold! It is the sacred duty of a householder to honor any guest who seeks shelter at his threshold, even if he be a bitter enemy! Preserve his life!'

The noble male dove immediately flew down to the roots and addressed the fowler: 'Welcome, honored guest! This tree is my home, and you are sheltered beneath my roof. Command me: how may I serve you?'

The fowler replied: 'I am freezing to death; provide me with fire!'

The dove flew to a nearby charcoal-burner's pit, retrieved a glowing ember in his beak, and dropped it upon a pile of dry leaves beneath the tree. Fanning the ember with his wings, he soon had a roaring, warm fire blazing on the hearth.

The fowler warmed his frozen limbs, but said: 'Now hunger torments my stomach; provide me with food!'

The poor dove had neither grain nor fruit in his nest. He reflected: 'A host who permits his guest to starve is condemned in this world and the next. My own body is all I possess.'

Flying three times around the fire in sacred pradakshina, the noble dove said: 'Honored guest, accept my body as your food!' With that, he plunged into the flames, roasting his flesh to feed his starving enemy!

Witnessing this sublime, unhesitating self-sacrifice, the cruel fowler was struck to his very soul with profound remorse. Tears poured down his weathered cheeks: 'What a vile, bloodthirsty monster have I been! This humble bird sacrificed his life to feed the wretch who imprisoned his mate!'

Weeping, the fowler opened the wicker cage and released the female dove. Seeing her mate burned to ashes in the coals, the grieving widow threw herself into the flames to join her husband in eternity.

The transformed fowler broke his nets, smashed his birdlime, renounced his cruel trade, and spent the remainder of his days in severe penance and charity, attaining spiritual redemption through the grace of the self-sacrificing dove.

Thus Vishnu Sharma taught:
"The host who offers up his life to warm a freezing guest,
And feeds his enemy with flesh from his unyielding breast,
Melts the cruel heart of stone to tears of penitence and grace,
And leaves an everlasting light upon his resting place."
moral: Supreme hospitality and self-sacrifice soften the hardest heart and redeem even the cruelest sinner.

title: The Old Man with the Young Wife
summary: In a wealthy manufacturing city lived an elderly merchant named Kamatura, who, despite his silver hair and wrinkled brow, married a young...
keywords: the old man with the young wife
full_text:
In a wealthy manufacturing city lived an elderly merchant named Kamatura, who, despite his silver hair and wrinkled brow, married a young and beautiful maiden named Ratnavati, purchasing her hand with an enormous dowry of gold and jewels.

Though the old husband showered her with silks, perfumes, and emeralds, the young bride felt only cold distaste for his infirmities. Whenever he sat beside her on the couch, she turned her back to him, shrinking to the far edge of the mattress and weeping in silence. For months, the old man pleaded for a single warm embrace, but in vain.

One dark midnight, while the couple lay sleeping on their couch—the bride turned cold and distant against the wall—a professional thief cut through the brickwork of the bedroom and slipped inside with a drawn dagger to steal the merchant's gold.

Waking from a light sleep, the young wife saw the dark silhouette of the armed thief standing beside the bed. Terrified out of her wits, she screamed, leaped across the couch, and wrapped both her arms passionately around her old husband's neck, clinging to his chest with all her might, trembling with fear!

Awakened by this unexpected, passionate embrace, the old merchant was filled with ecstatic joy. 'My beloved embraces me with such devotion!' he thought.

Looking up, he saw the thief standing in the shadows with the dagger.

The shrewd old merchant immediately understood the cause of her sudden warmth. Sitting up in bed, holding his clinging wife with one arm, he called out cheerfully to the thief: 'Welcome, noble benefactor! Come forward and take whatever gold, pearls, or silver pleases your heart! For months I have spent thousands of dinars seeking an embrace from this cold wife, and tonight your presence has won me what all my gold could not purchase! Take your reward and go in peace!'

The thief was so amused by the old man's wit and gratitude that he took only a small bag of silver and departed with a chuckle, leaving the old merchant rejoicing in his good fortune.

Thus Vishnu Sharma taught:
"An unexpected circumstance that fills the heart with fright
May yield the sweetest harvest in the shadow of the night;
The husband blessed the prowling thief who made his bride embrace,
And turned the terror of the knife to laughter in his place."
moral: Blessings sometimes arrive in the disguise of an intruder; even a thief may inadvertently render a service.

title: The Brahmin the Thief and the Ghost
summary: In a secluded forest hermitage lived an impoverished, austere Brahmin named Drona, who had renounced all worldly luxury. An admirer had p...
keywords: the brahmin the thief and the ghost
full_text:
In a secluded forest hermitage lived an impoverished, austere Brahmin named Drona, who had renounced all worldly luxury. An admirer had presented him with two young calves, which the holy man nourished with wild grass and clean spring water until they grew into two magnificent, sleek, muscular white bullocks.

A professional highway thief observed the fat animals and resolved: 'Tonight I will steal those two fine bullocks and sell them in the royal bazaar.'

As the thief was walking down the dark, wooded trail toward the hermitage, he encountered an awful specter: a terrifying ghost, or the ancient elder-Rakshasa, with hollow sunken eyes, fangs like sharp chisels, skin the color of dry smoke, and protruding ribs.

Though his hair stood on end, the thief asked: 'Who are you, terrifying apparition?'

The ghost replied: 'I am a hungry ghost who eats once every six nights. Tonight is my sixth night, and I am walking to the hermitage to devour the pious Brahmin Drona. Who are you?'

The thief felt his courage return: 'I am a thief! I am going to the same cottage to steal his two fat bullocks! Let us walk together.'

Arriving at the hermitage, they slipped through the bamboo wattle. The two fat bullocks were tethered peacefully under the thatched shed, while the pious Brahmin slept deeply on his grass mat on the veranda, exhausted from his day of chanting sacred texts.

The ghost stepped forward, extending his bony claws: 'Stand aside, thief! I will devour the Brahmin first while he is asleep!'

The thief seized the ghost's arm: 'No! If you attempt to seize him, he may utter a cry and wake the villagers! If the peasants rush in with clubs, I will not be able to drive off the cattle! Let me untie the bullocks and lead them into the road first, and then you may devour the Brahmin at your leisure!'

The ghost snarled: 'If you untie the cattle first, their clattering hooves will awaken the Brahmin! If he wakes, he will recite sacred mantras, and I will be burned to ashes! I will eat him now!'

'No, the cattle come first!' hissed the thief.

Their stubborn argument grew so loud and furious that the sleeping Brahmin sat up on his mat.

Seeing the holy man awake, the thief immediately shouted: 'Brahmin, beware! This hungry ghost has come to devour you!'

The ghost shrieked: 'Brahmin, beware! This thief has come to steal your two fat bullocks!'

Rising calmly from his mat, the Brahmin recited the powerful Gayatri and protective Vedic mantras. Hearing the sacred syllables, the ghost shrieked in agony and dissolved into the mist; while the Brahmin seized his heavy staff and drove the terrified thief out of the garden.

Thus Vishnu Sharma taught:
"When wicked thieves and hungry ghosts in mutual hatred clash,
Their secret enterprise dissolves like embers into ash;
The righteous man who keeps his faith and speaks the sacred word,
Finds safety from the quarreling foe before his voice is heard."
moral: When evil forces conspire against the virtuous, their own mutual jealousy frustrates their wicked intent.

title: The Snake in the Prince's Belly
summary: In a northern kingdom ruled a king whose eldest son was afflicted by an agonizing, mysterious internal malady: an infant serpent had slip...
keywords: the snake in the prince's belly
full_text:
In a northern kingdom ruled a king whose eldest son was afflicted by an agonizing, mysterious internal malady: an infant serpent had slipped into his mouth while he slept in a forest pavilion, growing within his stomach into a venomous snake that fed upon all the nourishment the prince consumed. The youth grew as gaunt as a skeleton, his skin yellow, unable to find cure from all the royal physicians.

In despair, the prince left his father's palace and wandered as an impoverished mendicant into a distant realm, taking shelter in the temple of a city ruled by King Varadev.

Now King Varadev had two daughters. Every morning, the elder daughter bowed to the king and said: 'Hail, Sire! By your favor alone do we enjoy wealth and happiness!' The younger daughter, however, was philosophical and said: 'Sire, each soul enjoys only the fruit of its own past karma!'

Enraged by the younger daughter's independence, the king shouted: 'Since you depend only upon your own karma, you shall marry the first beggar who passes the gate!' The king summoned the sick, emaciated prince from the temple porch and married the princess to him on the spot.

The virtuous princess accepted her husband with unyielding devotion. Renting an old bullock cart, she carried the dying prince toward a mountain climate, nursing him with water and prayers.

One hot noon, as the princess went to a village well to buy flour, the prince lay asleep in the cart beneath the shade of an ancient ant-hill.

From the prince's open mouth emerged the head of the serpent that dwelt in his stomach, breathing the fresh air. At the same moment, another venomous serpent emerged from a hole in the ant-hill.

Seeing each other, the two serpents began to quarrel with venomous spite.

The ant-hill serpent hissed: 'Shame upon you, wicked worm! Why do you torture the body of this noble young prince, draining his lifeblood?'

The stomach serpent retorted: 'And shame upon you, greedy wretch! You sit coiled over two massive cauldrons of pure gold buried in this ant-hill, guarding treasure you can never spend! If someone only poured hot mustard water down the prince's throat, you would be vomited forth and killed instantly!'

The ant-hill serpent hissed back: 'And if someone only poured boiling water mixed with ground neem leaves into this hole, you would be boiled alive, and they would dig up all your gold!'

Returning with her flour, the intelligent princess had hidden behind a bush and overheard every word of their mutual accusations.

Acting with swift decisiveness, the princess brewed a bowl of hot mustard water and poured it down her sleeping husband's throat. The internal serpent was vomited forth and instantly killed with a staff, restoring the prince to glowing health and strength!

She then poured boiling neem water into the ant-hill, destroying the second serpent, and unearthed the two cauldrons of gold!

Rich and radiant in health, the prince revealed his royal lineage, returned to his father's kingdom with his brilliant bride, and ruled in glory, having learned that enemies reveal their own destruction through their mutual hatred.

Thus Vishnu Sharma taught:
"When mutual adversaries meet and vent their bitter spleen,
They blab the hidden remedies that otherwise lie unseen;
The prudent ear that overhears the secrets of their wrath,
Finds gold and healing waiting sweet along the quiet path."
moral: Two adversaries possessing secret weaknesses can be made to destroy each other by one who overhears their secrets.

title: The Gullible Carpenter
summary: In a manufacturing town lived an industrious, skilled carpenter named Brihadbhadra, who adored his beautiful young wife with blind, dotin...
full_text:
In a manufacturing town lived an industrious, skilled carpenter named Brihadbhadra, who adored his beautiful young wife with blind, doting affection. The neighbors, however, whispered that the woman was unfaithful and entertained the town magistrate's son whenever her husband was absent.

Tormented by suspicion, the carpenter said to his wife: 'Dearest, I must travel to a distant village to fell timber for a temple, and I shall be absent for several days.'

Instead of departing, the carpenter slipped into his own bedroom at dusk and crawled beneath the low, carved wooden bedstead, hiding in the dark to discover the truth with his own eyes.

Believing her husband was miles away, the unfaithful wife sent for her lover. They feasted on sweets and wine, and at midnight lay down upon the bed.

As the lover shifted his weight, his foot slipped over the mattress and brushed against the concealed carpenter's hand beneath the bed!

The wife instantly recognized the rough, calloused touch of her husband's hand. In a flash of cunning presence of mind, she did not scream or panic. Instead, when her lover whispered words of affection, she pushed him away with cold dignity.

'Why do you reject my suit tonight, fair lady?' the lover asked in surprise.

The cunning wife raised her voice so that every syllable was clear to the man under the bed: 'Speak not to me of love, sir! Today, while praying at the temple of the Divine Mother, a celestial voice echoed from the sanctuary, saying: "Within three days, your devoted husband Brihadbhadra is destined to die of a sudden fever!"'

'I wept and begged the goddess: "Is there no remedy to avert my beloved husband's death?" The goddess replied: "If you lay upon your couch for one night with another man, your husband's fatal doom will pass away, and he will live in health for a hundred years!" That, sir, is why I permitted you to enter my house: to take upon yourself the fatal curse and save the life of the husband I adore more than my own soul!'

Hearing this brazen fabrication, the foolish carpenter under the bed was overwhelmed with tears of gratitude! 'What a saintly, devoted wife!' thought the dupe. 'She has sacrificed her honor to save my life!'

Crawling from beneath the bedstead, the weeping carpenter embraced his wife with kisses, bowed to her lover, and in his doting madness, carried both his wife and her lover upon his shoulders through the town square, shouting to his laughing neighbors that his wife was the most virtuous woman on earth!

Thus Vishnu Sharma taught:
"The doting fool who loves in vain and shuts his reason tight,
Will take the blackest, brazen fraud for pure, angelic light;
He carries on his foolish back the architect of shame,
And celebrates his own disgrace with an exalted name."
moral: A foolish husband who chooses to believe a brazen lie rather than his own eyes becomes a laughingstock.

title: Mouse-Maid Made Mouse
summary: On the banks of the sacred river Jahnavi, the revered sage Yajnavalkya stood waist-deep in the water, performing his morning prayers and ...
full_text:
On the banks of the sacred river Jahnavi, the revered sage Yajnavalkya stood waist-deep in the water, performing his morning prayers and offering libations of water to the rising sun.

Suddenly, a mountain hawk soaring above dropped a tiny, newborn female field-mouse from its talons. The tiny creature tumbled into the sage's cupped palms.

Moved by compassion for the helpless mite, the sage placed her on a leaf, purified her with sacred mantras, and through his immense yogic power, transformed the tiny mouse into a baby girl of heavenly beauty. Carrying the infant to his hermitage, he said to his childless wife: 'Accept this child, wife, and raise her as our own beloved daughter.'

For twelve years, the maiden grew into radiant grace, endowed with every virtue and modesty.

When she reached marriageable age, the sage said to his wife: 'Our daughter must wed a husband worthy of her celestial beauty. I will summon the mightiest power in the cosmos.'

The sage invoked the glorious Sun God. The radiant deity descended in his flaming chariot. The sage said: 'Noble Sun, accept my daughter in marriage!'

The sage asked the maiden: 'Do you desire the Sun God for your husband?'

The girl replied: 'Father, he is too fiery, burning, and harsh! I desire someone mightier than he!'

The sage asked the Sun: 'Is there anyone mightier than you?'

The Sun God replied: 'Yes, the great Cloud is mightier than I, for he covers my face and dims my light with his shadows.'

The sage invoked the Rain Cloud, who appeared in dark majesty. But the maiden said: 'He is too dark, cold, and stormy! Seek someone mightier!'

The Cloud said: 'The Wind God is mightier than I, for he drives me across the heavens at his whim.'

The sage summoned the Wind God. But the maiden rejected him, saying: 'He is too restless, wandering, and unstable!'

The Wind God said: 'The mighty Mountain is mightier than I, for his granite peaks stand unyielding against my fiercest hurricanes.'

The sage summoned the Mountain God, standing tall and unshakeable. But the maiden sighed: 'He is too rigid, hard, and stony!'

The sage asked the Mountain: 'Is there anyone mightier than you?'

The Mountain smiled: 'Yes, the tiny field-mouse is mightier than I, for with his sharp teeth, he burrows into my foundations and shatters my granite rocks from within!'

The sage invoked a handsome young field-mouse, who hopped onto the veranda, twitching his whiskers.

The moment the maiden saw the mouse, her heart fluttered with innate, uncontrollable joy! Her eyes sparkled, and she cried out: 'Father! Father! Choose this one! Make me a mouse, so that I may dwell happily with my own kind!'

Smiling at the unalterable law of nature, the sage sprinkled holy water upon her head, saying: 'Return to your true nature, little daughter!'

She transformed back into a sleek, happy mouse and scurried off with her mate into the meadows.

Thus Vishnu Sharma taught:
"Though magic clothe a humble soul with beauty and renown,
And offer for her bridal bed the monarch's golden crown,
The inborn nature of the heart will claim its native place,
And seek its joy among the kind that matches with its race."
moral: One's innate nature and destiny cannot be altered by outer magic; what is born of a kind returns to its kind.

title: The Bird with Golden Dung
summary: Upon the soaring summit of Mount Mandara, high above the clouds, dwelt a celestial bird named Sindhuka whose golden droppings turned to p...
full_text:
Upon the soaring summit of Mount Mandara, high above the clouds, dwelt a celestial bird named Sindhuka whose golden droppings turned to pure gold the instant they touched the earth. A mountain hunter wandered into the crags and witnessed the miraculous bird perched upon an acacia bough, dropping a glistening pellet that immediately hardened into an ingot of heavy gold.

Stunned by greed, the fowler set an invisible horsehair snare among the branches. When Sindhuka alighted to peck mountain berries, his talons were ensnared. Carrying the marvelous prize to his hut, the hunter gloated: 'I am the richest man in Bharatavarsha!' Yet fear soon overtook him: 'If my neighbors notice my sudden wealth, they will whisper to the royal tax collectors. The king will accuse me of stealing royal treasure and execute me.'

Resolving to win royal favor instead, the hunter presented Sindhuka to King Amaradatta, proclaiming its miraculous power. Delighted, the king rewarded the hunter with lands and ordered the bird housed in a golden aviary, served milk and sugared almonds. Yet the king's jealous chief minister sneered: 'Sire, how can you believe a lowly fowler's fantasy? No bird in creation ever dropped gold! This hunter mocks your majesty. Open the cage and let the worthless fowl go.'

The gullible king believed his minister and ordered Sindhuka released. The instant the cage door swung wide, Sindhuka fluttered upward and perched securely upon the high marble cornice of the royal council hall. Looking down upon the foolish sovereign and his arrogant court, the bird dropped a gleaming pellet of gold that struck the palace flagstones with a bright metallic chime.

Laughing in clear, human speech, Sindhuka said: 'First was I a fool to trust the hunter's tree; second was the hunter a fool to surrender golden fortune for mere silver; but the greatest fool is the king who cast away a jewel of heaven upon the word of a jealous counselor!' With that, the golden bird spread his wings and vanished into the mountain mist. As Vishnu Sharma noted:
"He who rejects a treasure that has fallen to his hand
Believing jealous flatterers who cannot understand,
Shall weep with empty fingers when the golden bird has flown,
And reap the bitter harvest of the folly he has sown."
moral: He who rejects an impossible fortune upon the word of a jealous courtier loses the treasure he held in his hand.

title: The Cave That Talked
summary: In a rugged mountain valley, a ferocious old lion named Kharanakhara roamed from dawn till twilight in search of prey, but his joints wer...
full_text:
In a rugged mountain valley, a ferocious old lion named Kharanakhara roamed from dawn till twilight in search of prey, but his joints were stiff and no deer crossed his path. Famished and exhausted as the sun dipped behind the purple ridges, he stumbled upon an enormous, cool cave in the limestone cliffs.

'Surely some fat beast dwells in this shelter,' thought the predator. 'I shall conceal myself in the deepest shadows near the wall and wait. When the tenant returns at nightfall to sleep, I will leap upon him and feast.' The lion tucked his paws, silenced his breathing, and waited in the darkness.

The cavern was the home of an exceptionally shrewd jackal named Dadhipuchha. As the moon rose, the jackal trotted toward his home, humming softly. Arriving at the entrance, his sharp eyes noticed deep claw marks pressed into the damp soil—tracks leading directly into the cave mouth, but none leading out!

Dadhipuchha froze. 'A predator is inside my den,' he deduced. 'If I enter blindly, I am a corpse. Yet if an innocent guest took shelter and I abandon my home, I lose my sanctuary for nothing. I must test the silence.'

Stepping back to a safe distance, the jackal cleared his throat and called out loudly: 'O Cave! O Cave! Why are you so silent tonight? Have you forgotten our sacred compact? Every night when I return from my foraging, you call out to welcome me: "Enter, friend Dadhipuchha, all is peaceful within!" Why do you refuse to speak tonight? If you do not answer me as you always do, I shall leave and take another dwelling across the valley!'

Huddled in the dark, the foolish lion heard the call and reasoned: 'This cave must truly be accustomed to answering its master every evening! If it remains silent now out of fear of my royal majesty, the jackal will depart and I will starve. I shall answer in the cave's place!'

Drawing a deep breath, the lion unleashed a colossal roar: 'ENTER, DADHIPUCHHA, ENTER IN PEACE!' The thunderous bellow shook the cliff walls, dislodged stones, and sent roosting bats shrieking into the night sky. Miles away, the forest animals trembled in terror.

Dadhipuchha laughed aloud: 'O clever cave! A cave that roars with the voice of a lion is a marvel I have never seen!' Hopping swiftly onto the forest trail, the jackal sprinted into the moonlight, saving his life through pure presence of mind. As Vishnu Sharma taught:
"He who encounters danger with a swift, observing mind
Uncovers hidden perils that the hasty leave behind;
A fool reveals his hiding place when vanity takes hold,
While wisdom turns the sharpest snare to safety ten times told."
moral: Observation of footprints reveals hidden danger; presence of mind saves the alert from the predator's trap.

title: The Frog That Rode Snakeback
summary: In a secluded marsh lived an old, exhausted water-snake named Mandavishya. With advancing age, his venom had weakened, his scales had dul...
full_text:
In a secluded marsh lived an old, exhausted water-snake named Mandavishya. With advancing age, his venom had weakened, his scales had dulled, and his speed was gone, so that he could no longer catch the agile green frogs in the lily ponds. Starving and desperate, he curled himself upon a grassy mound near the pond, sighing with feigned sorrow.

The king of the frogs, named Jalapada, surfaced near the bank and asked with surprise: 'Serpent, why do you lie so meekly upon the grass, refusing to chase my subjects?'

The snake replied with humble reverence: 'Alas, King Jalapada! I am undergoing severe penance for my past sins. Yesterday, while pursuing a frog into a Brahmin's hut, I mistakenly bit the foot of a pious young scholar, who died of my venom. His grieving father cursed me: "Because you struck my blameless son, you shall lose all your strength and venom! Henceforth, you shall be the humble vehicle of frogs, carrying them upon your back through the ponds, and you shall eat only what their king graciously bestows upon you as charity!" That, Sire, is why I have come to offer my services as your royal mount!'

Flattered by the idea of riding upon his hereditary predator, the vain frog king climbed out of the pond and hopped onto the snake's broad neck, accompanied by his chief ministers. The snake swam smoothly across the lotus pond, giving the frogs a delightful and dignified ride.

For several days, King Jalapada rode upon the snake, boasting of his supremacy to all the marsh creatures.

Presently, the snake slowed down, panting with exhaustion. 'Why do you move so slowly today, mount?' asked the frog king.

The snake sighed: 'Sire, I am starving. Your majesty has bestowed no charity upon me, and without food, I have no strength to swim.'

The vain frog king replied: 'Very well! You may eat one common frog from the rear of the herd every morning!'

Delighted, the treacherous snake began devouring frogs daily, growing fat and glossy.

When all the common frogs had been devoured, the snake turned his fangs upon the ministers, devouring them one by one. Finally, finding himself alone upon the snake's back, King Jalapada realized the terrible cost of his vanity.

Before the frog king could leap into the water, the serpent snapped his head back, swallowed the foolish monarch in a single gulp, and rested satisfied upon the bank.

Thus Vishnu Sharma taught:
"He who invites his mortal foe to serve his vain parade,
And trades his people's living flesh to keep his dignity displayed,
Shall find the mount he thought a slave turn hungry fangs in wrath,
And swallow down the foolish king along his watery path."
moral: He who allies with his hereditary enemy to destroy his rivals will himself be devoured in the end.

title: The Butter-blinded Brahmin
summary: In the fertile village of Patalika, a greedy and short-tempered Brahmin named Devasarman was obsessed with accumulating wealth and hoardi...
full_text:
In the fertile village of Patalika, a greedy and short-tempered Brahmin named Devasarman was obsessed with accumulating wealth and hoarding fine foods. Having performed a domestic ritual for a merchant, he was rewarded with a large earthenware jar filled to the brim with rich, freshly churned cow's ghee—sweet, golden, and fragrant.

Carrying the jar upon his shoulder, Devasarman hurried to his home, sealed all the wooden shutters, and locked his doors so that no guest, beggar, or neighboring child could ask for a taste. Sitting cross-legged upon his mat, he placed the heavy jar upon a brazier of burning coals to melt the butter into pure golden liquid, intending to gorge himself in absolute secrecy.

As the golden ghee bubbled with rich steam, his greed overwhelmed his patience. Without waiting for the scalding oil to cool, he leaned his face directly over the steaming rim, plunged a heavy ladle into the boiling cauldron, and gulped it down. In his frantic haste, the boiling grease spattered over his eyelids, scalding his face and burning his eyes with blinding agony.

Howling in pain, Devasarman leaped up, knocked the jar against the wall, and shattered the pottery to pieces. The hot melted butter poured across the hearth and caught fire, igniting the dry thatch of his roof. Blinded and weeping, the greedy Brahmin had to be dragged from his burning house by the neighbors he had refused to feed, his sight damaged and his wealth reduced to ashes.

Standing in the smoldering ruins, the humbled man confessed his shame. Thus Vishnu Sharma warned:
"He who is blinded by his greed and gorges in the dark,
Ignoring caution, patience, and the warning ember's spark,
Destroys the very prize he sought, and in his selfish haste
Beholds his home and fortune turned to ashes and to waste."
moral: Hasty greed that devours in secret without patience destroys the very prize it sought to hoard.

title: Loss of Gains (Frame - Monkey and Crocodile)
summary: Revered Vishnu Sharma opened the fourth scroll of wisdom: Labdhapranasham, the loss of hard-won treasures. 'Hearken, noble princes,' spok...
keywords: loss of gains (frame - monkey and crocodile)
full_text:
Revered Vishnu Sharma opened the fourth scroll of wisdom: Labdhapranasham, the loss of hard-won treasures. 'Hearken, noble princes,' spoke the sage. 'He who amasses wealth or wins a faithful friend, yet allows foolish complacence or treacherous deceit to blind his eyes, loses both treasure and friendship, like the foolish crocodile who sought to steal the monkey's heart.'

On the banks of the great Southern Ocean stood a colossal, spreading rose-apple tree whose boughs dipped over the sparkling salt water, heavy year-round with sweet, ruby-red jambu fruits. Inhabiting this leafy canopy was an exceptionally agile and wise monkey named Raktamukha, or Red-Face.

One sunny morning, a large, elderly crocodile named Karalamukha, or Terrible-Jaws, hauled his scaly bulk onto the sandy spit beneath the tree to rest. Seeing the weary aquatic beast, the generous monkey plucked a cluster of ripe, luscious rose-apples and tossed them down.

The crocodile tasted the fruit and was enchanted by its honeyed sweetness. Every day thereafter, the crocodile returned to the spit; Red-Face showered him with the sweetest fruits, and the two formed a warm, intimate brotherhood, conversing on the wonders of sea and land.

One evening, the crocodile carried a bundle of fresh rose-apples home to his wife in their subterranean sea cavern. The female crocodile tasted the fruit and asked: 'Husband, where did you find such heavenly nectar?'

The crocodile replied: 'My dear friend, the noble monkey who dwells in the rose-apple tree, gives them to me daily out of love.'

Greed and envy seized the wife's cruel heart: 'If a creature feeds daily on fruits of such divine sweetness, his own heart must be purer, sweeter, and more delicious than ambrosia! Bring that monkey to our cavern, husband! I must eat his sweet heart, or I will starve myself to death!'

The crocodile was horrified: 'Shame upon you, wife! He is my sworn brother who nourishes me daily! How can I betray a friend who trusts in my honor?'

The wife wept and raged, threatening to drown herself unless her wish was granted. Weakened by uxorious affection, the miserable crocodile yielded.

Swimming back to the tree, Terrible-Jaws put on a cheerful countenance: 'Brother Red-Face! My wife has heard of your boundless generosity and reproaches me for never bringing you to our home! Come, mount upon my back; I will carry you across the waves to our crystal cavern, where we will feast upon ocean delicacies!'

The trusting monkey agreed: 'I cannot swim, but I will gladly ride your back!'

Red-Face climbed onto the crocodile's broad, scaly back, and the great beast plunged into the deep waves. As they reached the middle of the ocean, where the water was black and shore was far behind, the crocodile began to sink beneath the surface.

Frightened, the monkey cried: 'Brother! Why do you sink? Keep your back high, or the salt water will drown me!'

Unable to conceal his guilt, the weeping crocodile confessed: 'Alas, brother! Forgive my treachery! My wicked wife demands your sweet heart to eat, and I am carrying you to your death!'

A cold chill struck the monkey's soul, but he knew that panic meant certain destruction. In a flash of brilliant presence of mind, he laughed heartily: 'Is that all, brother? Why did you not tell me before we left the shore? It would be the greatest honor to surrender my heart to your noble wife! But we monkeys never carry our hearts inside our chests when traveling over water; they would be soaked and ruined by salt spray! I left my heart hanging safely in the hollow of the rose-apple tree! Turn back immediately, swim to the tree, and I will fetch my heart to present to your wife!'

Believing the monkey's tale, the foolish crocodile turned around and swam with all his might back to the shore.

The instant the crocodile's snout touched the sand, Red-Face leaped from his back, scrambled up the rough bark of the rose-apple tree like lightning, and perched upon the highest, safest bough, breathing a deep sigh of relief!

Waiting below, the crocodile called out: 'Brother, fetch your heart, and let us return!'

The monkey pelted him with a hard fruit and laughed in scorn: 'Foolish monster! Did anyone ever hear of a living creature keeping his heart hanging on a tree branch? You are as stupid as you are treacherous! Begone to your sea cavern, and never return! A fool who has escaped a trap does not walk into it a second time!'

Weeping in shame and defeat, the crocodile slunk back into the ocean, having lost both his friend and his honor.

Thus Vishnu Sharma taught:
"The treasure won with patient toil and guarded with delight
Dissolves like mist when foolish trust admits the hypocrite;
Yet he who keeps his presence of mind when trapped in perilous deep,
Can make the predator turn back and his own freedom keep."
moral: He who loses his gains through treachery can recover his life through quick-witted presence of mind.

title: The Monkey and the Crocodile (detailed)
summary: After Red-Face the monkey had escaped the jaws of Karalamukha the crocodile and ascended safely to his rose-apple tree, the miserable rep...
full_text:
After Red-Face the monkey had escaped the jaws of Karalamukha the crocodile and ascended safely to his rose-apple tree, the miserable reptile floated in the surf below for many days, starving and filled with self-reproach.

Hoping to restore their lost friendship, the crocodile called upward in a mournful, flattering voice: 'Beloved brother Red-Face! Why do you look upon me with such cold suspicion? My words in the ocean were merely a test of your courage! My wife holds you in the highest esteem and awaits you with a garland of pearls! Forgive my rough jest, descend from the bough, and let us embrace in eternal brotherhood!'

Perched high among the green leaves, the monkey looked down with piercing eyes and spoke with firm, unshakeable wisdom: 'Hearken, Karalamukha! He who is deceived once by a treacherous villain is an unfortunate innocent; but he who is deceived twice by the same villain is a brainless fool! You proved yourself a traitor who broke the sacred bond of hospitality; why should I trust your honeyed words?'

The crocodile argued: 'Can a single error destroy years of mutual devotion? Return to me, and I swear by the sacred Ocean that no harm shall befall you!'

Red-Face replied with classic philosophical verse:
"The broken clay pot may be glued with wax and bitumen,
Yet the dark fracture line remains to mark what it had been;
The friendship severed by the knife of cold, deliberate spite,
Can never mend its shattered trust to walk within the light.

'Go, return to your treacherous wife, crocodile! If you linger beneath my tree, I will summon the village hunters with their iron harpoons to turn your hide into shields!'

Realizing that his deceit was utterly defeated by the monkey's unwavering prudence, the crocodile plunged into the dark waves and vanished forever.

Thus Vishnu Sharma taught:
"He who renews an old compact with one who sought his life,
Invites the treacherous blade again to cut him in the strife;
Turn from the flatterer's false tears, and bar your fortress door,
Lest foolish mercy bring your blood upon the slaughter floor."
moral: Do not renew an alliance with one who has already attempted your destruction.

title: Handsome and Theodore
summary: In a deep, masonry-lined irrigation well lived a community of green frogs ruled by their king, Gangadatta, or Handsome. Afflicted by the ...
full_text:
In a deep, masonry-lined irrigation well lived a community of green frogs ruled by their king, Gangadatta, or Handsome. Afflicted by the insolent disobedience and bitter mockery of his arrogant cousins and rival relatives, Handsome burned with a desire for revenge.

One morning, climbing to the stone coping by clinging to mossy cracks, the frog king hopped into the meadow, resolved to find an ally to destroy his insolent kin.

Near the well, he found an ancient, venomous black cobra named Priyadarsana, or Theodore, coiled outside his burrow. Trembling with fear yet driven by spite, the frog king called from a safe distance: 'Greetings, noble serpent! I am King Gangadatta! I offer you an alliance of mutual profit!'

The cobra hissed in astonishment: 'A frog seeks alliance with a serpent? You are my natural food; what alliance can exist between the eater and the eaten?'

Handsome replied: 'I know our natures are opposed, but I have a kingdom in yonder deep well. My wicked relatives torment me; if you enter the well, you may devour all my enemies one by one, while I live in peace as sovereign!'

The cobra reflected: 'I am old, and hunting in the open field is difficult. In that enclosed stone well, frogs cannot escape; it will be an effortless banquet!'

The cobra agreed to the compact. Gangadatta led the serpent to the well, and Theodore slithered down the mossy brickwork into the damp cavities above the water.

Day after day, Handsome pointed out his rival relatives: 'Eat that one today, friend Theodore! Eat those two tomorrow!' The cobra struck and swallowed the frog king's cousins, uncles, and rivals until not a single enemy remained alive in the well.

Handsome rejoiced, saying: 'Brother Theodore, you have fulfilled your compact! All my rivals are destroyed. Now climb back to your field and enjoy your freedom.'

The cobra laughed with cold, sinister mockery: 'Climb back? My outdoor burrow has been taken over by mongooses while I was here! I have grown accustomed to this cool well and effortless meals! You brought me here, Handsome, and it is your duty to feed me! Point out more frogs, or I will devour you and your children!'

Paralyzed by remorse, Handsome realized the fatal trap he had built with his own spite. To preserve his own life, he was forced to surrender his loyal friends, then his ministers, and finally his own beloved sons to the serpent's belly!

When only Handsome and his queen remained, the cobra hissed: 'Handsome, who shall be my breakfast tomorrow?'

Handsome replied with feigned humility: 'Noble friend, let me climb out of the well. I will visit neighboring ponds and persuade other frog colonies to enter this wonderful well, promising them safety, so that you may feast forever!'

Delighted by the prospect of endless prey, the foolish snake permitted Handsome to climb out of the well.

The instant Handsome reached the green meadow, he took giant leaps toward a distant, deep river!

Waiting in the dry well, the hungry snake called up to a lizard passing the coping: 'Go to Handsome and tell him to return with the frogs; I miss his sweet company!'

The lizard carried the message. Handsome laughed from the safe riverbank:
"Tell the black serpent Theodore, who coils within the pit,
That Handsome has recovered all his reason and his wit;
He who enters the serpent's mouth to settle petty spite,
Will never walk into the trap a second time by night!"

Thus Vishnu Sharma taught:
"He who invites a deadlier foe to crush his kinsman's pride,
Shall see the monster swallow up his children at his side;
Seek not the foreign tyrant's aid to heal a domestic sore,
Lest his insatiate appetite consume you evermore."
moral: He who brings a deadly enemy into his own household to settle domestic grudges is destroyed by his own weapon.

title: Flop-Ear and Dusty
summary: In a bustling town lived an impoverished washerman named Shuddhaka. To assist him in his trade, he kept two domestic animals: an ancient,...
full_text:
In a bustling town lived an impoverished washerman named Shuddhaka. To assist him in his trade, he kept two domestic animals: an ancient, emaciated donkey named Flop-Ear, who carried heavy bundles of soiled linen to the river daily, and a lean guard dog named Dusty, who guarded the courtyard by night.

One midnight, while the exhausted washerman was snoring heavily upon his cot, a professional thief scaled the garden wall and crept toward the shed where the clean, ironed silk garments were stored.

Flop-Ear the donkey saw the thief slipping through the shadows. Turning to Dusty the dog, who was lying curled asleep in the dust, the donkey hissed: 'Brother Dusty! Look, a thief has entered our master's premises! Why do you not bark with all your might to awaken him?'

Dusty opened one lazy eye and yawned: 'Mind your own business, Flop-Ear! For months, our master has lived in safety, and because no danger threatened, he has neglected to feed me, tossing me only dry crusts and bones! Only when danger strikes do masters remember the value of faithful guardians! Let the thief steal a bundle; when the master feels the sting of loss, he will appreciate my vigilance and feed me rich meat!'

Flop-Ear was indignant: 'Shame upon you, ungrateful wretch! He who neglects his duty in the hour of peril is a traitor! If you will not bark, I will raise the alarm myself!'

The dog warned: 'Do not interfere, Flop-Ear! Braying is not your office!'

Ignoring the dog's wise counsel, the donkey lifted his long muzzle toward the moon and began to bray with all his might: 'HEE-HAW! HEE-HAW! HEE-HAW!'

The deafening, discordant noise shattered the silence of the night, echoing through the courtyard like a rusty iron hinge.

Startled by the racket, the thief leaped over the wall and escaped into the dark.

The washerman woke from his sweet sleep, his head throbbing with a headache. Stumbling into the courtyard armed with a heavy wooden washing mallet, he looked around and saw no thief, but only Flop-Ear braying frantically in his stall.

Enraged at having his rest destroyed for no apparent reason, the furious washerman raised his heavy mallet and beat poor Flop-Ear across his back, ribs, and legs until the donkey collapsed groaning upon the manure heap.

Dusty the dog curled up again and remarked:
"He who assumes another's post and meddles in his trade,
Expecting grateful gratitude for services displayed,
Shall find the mallet of reward break down his aching frame,
And learn that uninvited zeal brings only blows and shame."
moral: Do not neglect your own duty to meddle in another's office; an uninvited service brings only a beating.

title: The Potter Militant
summary: In a quiet village lived an honest, impoverished potter named Yudhishthira. One night, having consumed a pot of strong palm liquor, he st...
full_text:
In a quiet village lived an honest, impoverished potter named Yudhishthira. One night, having consumed a pot of strong palm liquor, he stumbled across his yard in the dark, tripped over a heap of broken pottery sherds, and struck his forehead against the jagged rim of a broken storage jar. The sharp shard sliced deep into his brow, producing a massive, jagged, terrifying scar across his forehead.

A terrible famine struck the province. Abandoning his wheel, the potter traveled to the royal capital and enlisted among the King's hired soldiers.

When the King reviewed his new recruits, his eyes fell upon Yudhishthira. Seeing the colossal, jagged scar across the man's brow, the monarch thought: 'Look at that formidable warrior! That scar could only have been inflicted by a frontal blow from a heavy broadsword or battle-axe in some desperate war! He must be a hero of extraordinary valor!'

The King immediately elevated the humble potter above seasoned veterans, granting him high rank, fine silks, warhorses, and commanding office in the royal guard. The true warriors murmured with jealousy, but the potter held his tongue, enjoying his unearned glory.

A year later, a neighboring emperor invaded the realm with war-elephants, archers, and armored cavalry. The King mobilized his army and appointed the 'scarred hero' to lead the vanguard into battle.

As the war-drums thundered and the soldiers strapped on their armor, Yudhishthira began to tremble uncontrollably. His teeth chattered, his knees shook, and he could scarcely hold his lance.

Noticing his champion's sudden panic, the King rode up and asked privately: 'Noble hero! You who bear the scar of a hundred desperate combats, why do your limbs tremble before the battle?'

Cornered by impending slaughter, the terrified potter confessed the truth: 'Sire! I am no warrior, but a humble village potter! This scar on my forehead was not won in battle against heroes; I was drunk on palm wine, slipped in the dark, and cut my brow upon a broken earthen jar!'

The King was stunned, but smiled at the man's honest confession: 'You have deceived me, potter, but your truth has saved my army from defeat under a cowardly commander! Slip quietly away from the battlefield and return to your clay wheel before my veteran warriors discover your secret and tear you to pieces!'

Thanking the King for his life, the potter threw down his spear, stripped off his armor, and ran back to his village, happy to shape humble clay in peace.

Thus Vishnu Sharma taught:
"Though unearned honors crown your brow and place you with the brave,
The fiery test of actual strife strips bare the boasting knave;
Retreat in time from false renown before the battle cries,
And find within your honest trade the peace that pride denies."
moral: Borrowed reputation cannot withstand the fiery test of actual battle; retreat in time before false pride destroys you.

title: The Jackal Who defeated No Elephants
summary: In a mountain cavern dwelt a ferocious lion and his noble mate. One spring, the lioness gave birth to two healthy, golden lion cubs. Ever...
keywords: the jackal who defeated no elephants
full_text:
In a mountain cavern dwelt a ferocious lion and his noble mate. One spring, the lioness gave birth to two healthy, golden lion cubs. Every morning, the lion hunted deer and wild buffalo, laying the choice meats before the cavern to nourish his family.

One afternoon, having roamed the hills without finding game, the lion came upon a newborn, abandoned jackal pup shivering in the grass. Moved by fatherly compassion, the lion carried the tiny creature gently between his teeth and placed it beside his own cubs.

The lioness nursed the jackal pup alongside her two sons. The three grew up together as loving brothers, knowing no difference between them.

One day, as the three young beasts roamed the valley, a colossal wild bull elephant in rut crashed through the bamboo thickets, trumpeting with earth-shattering fury.

The two young lion cubs bristled their golden manes, crouched low, and prepared to leap upon the elephant with flashing claws, roaring: 'Look, brothers! Here is magnificent prey!'

The young jackal, however, seized by his ancestral instinct of terror, shrieked in panic: 'Brothers, run! Run for your lives! That monster will crush us to dust!' He turned his tail and sprinted back to the cave in terrified flight.

Seeing their elder brother flee, the two lion cubs hesitated, lost their momentum, and followed him back to the den.

At the cavern, the two lion cubs laughed at the jackal: 'Father, mother! Our elder brother was so terrified of an elephant that his tail tucked into his belly and he ran like a frightened hare!'

Hearing their mockery, the young jackal turned purple with rage: 'Insolent cubs! Do you dare to mock my courage? I will tear both of your throats out!'

The wise lioness called the jackal aside into a private chamber and said gently: 'Listen to me, my child. You are handsome, you are intelligent, and you have been raised with royal dignity upon lion's milk. But your ancestors were jackals, not lions! In your race, no one has ever defeated an elephant! Before your brothers grow old enough to realize you are not of their blood and tear you to pieces, slip away into the southern plains, join your own kind, and live in safety!'

Realizing the truth of his nature, the young jackal thanked his foster mother, departed quietly for the plains, and lived happily among his fellow jackals.

Thus Vishnu Sharma taught:
"Though raised on royal nectar and adorned with noble grace,
A creature cannot transcend the blood and nature of his race;
Know your own strength, your limits, and your heritage with pride,
Lest foolish imitation bring your destruction at your side."
moral: Know your innate capacities; do not boast of warrior prowess when your nature is not made for battle.
